nodes.title: Hittite Religion
nodes.summary: The multilingual state and local cults of Bronze Age Hatti in central Anatolia.
nodes.content:
# Hittite Religion

## Historical context

Hittite archives from Hattusa preserve thousands of ritual, festival, mythic, and diplomatic tablets from second-millennium BCE Anatolia. Court scribes worked in Hittite, Hattic, Hurrian, Luwian, Akkadian, and other languages. The famous phrase “the thousand gods of Hatti” reflects deliberate incorporation of local and foreign cults rather than a single stable pantheon imposed throughout the kingdom.

## Distinctives and comparative notes

Seasonal festivals, oath gods, royal ancestor rites, purification, sacrifice, and careful maintenance of divine images tied ritual accuracy to political welfare. Hurrian deities and narratives became especially influential at court, while older Anatolian elements persisted. The influence edge denotes documented translation and cult transfer. Comparisons between the Kumarbi cycle and Greek succession myths are valuable, although transmission routes and intermediate traditions remain debated.

outbound.title: Hurrian Religion
outbound.citation: Gary Beckman, The Religion of the Hittites, Biblical Archaeologist 52 (1989)

nodes.title: Hòa Hảo Buddhism
nodes.summary: A Vietnamese Buddhist reform religion founded by Huỳnh Phú Sổ in the Mekong Delta, emphasizing accessible household practice and social ethics.
nodes.content:
# Hòa Hảo Buddhism

## Historical context

Huỳnh Phú Sổ began preaching in 1939 in the western Mekong Delta, building on the earlier Bửu Sơn Kỳ Hương reform environment. The movement grew rapidly among rural communities and became entangled in anticolonial conflict, armed politics, and the founder’s disappearance in 1947. Hòa Hảo institutions survived warfare, diaspora, and changing state regulation.

## Distinctives and comparative notes

Hòa Hảo teaching encourages Buddhist moral reform, simple home altars, remembrance of ancestors, charity, and reduced dependence on costly ceremonies or monastic intermediaries. Its plain brown altar cloth and emphasis on inward sincerity express a rural reform ethic. It is a self-identifying Buddhist tradition with a particular Vietnamese history, not merely “folk Buddhism” or a political faction.

nodes.title: Hoodoo / African American Conjure
nodes.summary: An African American healing, protection, divination, and justice practice complex rather than a single church or uniform religion.
nodes.content:
# Hoodoo / African American Conjure

## Historical context

Hoodoo developed among enslaved African Americans and their descendants, especially in the southern United States, through Central and West African knowledge, biblical practice, Indigenous and European materia, and the conditions of racial violence. Emancipation, migration, commercial spiritual-supply shops, folklore collecting, and popular media changed how techniques circulated.

## Distinctives and comparative notes

Rootworkers may use herbs, roots, minerals, personal concerns, prayer, Psalms, amulets, baths, and divination for healing, luck, protection, love, or justice. Hoodoo has often been practiced by Christians and does not require membership in a separate religion. It should not be confused with Haitian Vodou, and commercial “spell” stereotypes obscure its African American history and community ethics.

nodes.title: Hopi Religion
nodes.summary: Community-governed religious traditions of Hopi villages in what is now northeastern Arizona.
nodes.content:
# Hopi Religion

## Historical context

Hopi villages maintain distinct clan histories, ceremonial societies, agricultural knowledge, and responsibilities rooted in long residence on and around the Hopi mesas. Spanish missions, United States rule, schooling, land disputes, tourism, and media intrusion have affected religious life. Much knowledge is restricted by community authority, so publicly available ethnography does not license outsiders to reproduce ceremonies or secret narratives.

## Distinctives and comparative notes

Dry farming, rain, emergence histories, katsinam, pilgrimage, reciprocity, and village ceremonial cycles connect ethical life with place. Practice differs among villages and societies; “Hopi religion” is not a single public creed. New Age prophecy literature frequently detaches Hopi teachings from custodianship and sometimes invents quotations. Comparative study should honor Hopi decisions about what may be shared and avoid turning living responsibilities into generic environmental symbolism.

nodes.title: Huayan Buddhism
nodes.summary: An East Asian Mahāyāna tradition centered on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra and the interpenetration of all phenomena.
nodes.content:
# Huayan Buddhism

## Historical context

Huayan scholastic identity developed in medieval China around successive translations of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* and exegetes later arranged as patriarchs, especially Zhiyan, Fazang, and Chengguan. Court patronage supported sophisticated systems classifying Buddhist teachings. Independent Huayan institutions declined after the Tang, but its philosophy entered Chan, Tiantai, Pure Land, Korean Hwaeom, and Japanese Kegon traditions.

## Distinctives and comparative notes

Huayan thinkers describe every phenomenon as dependently arising within and interpenetrating every other without erasing distinction, illustrated through Indra’s net and Fazang’s golden lion. The bodhisattva’s path is interpreted through a cosmos already pervaded by buddhahood. Popular summaries sometimes turn interpenetration into a vague claim that “everything is one”; Huayan instead develops precise accounts of relation, emptiness, difference, and ethical practice.

nodes.title: Humanistic Buddhism
nodes.summary: A modern Chinese Buddhist current emphasizing this-worldly practice, education, welfare, culture, and the bodhisattva path in everyday life.
nodes.content:
# Humanistic Buddhism

## Historical context

Twentieth-century reformer Taixu promoted a “Buddhism for human life,” and Yin Shun further developed the language of Buddhism for the human realm. Later organizations in Taiwan and the Chinese diaspora—including Fo Guang Shan, Dharma Drum Mountain, and Tzu Chi—translated related ideals into education, charity, media, cultural work, and lay participation. These institutions remain organizationally independent and interpret the current differently.

## Distinctives and comparative notes

Humanistic Buddhism locates the bodhisattva path in ordinary society rather than treating Buddhism chiefly as funerary ritual or escape from the world. It values ethical action, accessible teaching, community service, and the possibility of creating a Pure Land through transformed relationships. Its modern institutions use management and technology, but the movement grounds this adaptation in Mahāyāna precedents rather than presenting secular humanitarianism as a replacement for awakening.

nodes.title: Hurrian Religion
nodes.summary: Religious traditions of Hurrian-speaking communities across northern Mesopotamia, Syria, and Anatolia.
nodes.content:
# Hurrian Religion

## Historical context

Hurrian-speaking peoples lived across a wide zone from northern Mesopotamia to Syria and Anatolia during the third and second millennia BCE. Their traditions are reconstructed from archives at Hattusa, Ugarit, Nuzi, and other sites, often through texts copied by non-Hurrian scribes. Political formations such as Mittani mattered, but no single Hurrian state or priesthood defined all practice.

## Distinctives and comparative notes

The storm god Teššub, Ḫebat, Šauška, Kumarbi, and deities grouped as ancient “former gods” feature in surviving myth and ritual. Offerings, purification, music, divination, and oath-making traveled through multilingual courts. Hurrian compositions shaped Hittite archives and may stand within longer routes toward Greek myth, but missing intermediaries caution against simple one-to-one descent. Local Syrian and Anatolian traditions also transformed what they received.

inbound.title: Hittite Religion
inbound.citation: Gary Beckman, The Religion of the Hittites, Biblical Archaeologist 52 (1989)

nodes.title: Ibadi Islam
nodes.summary: An early Islamic tradition distinct from Sunni and Shi'a Islam, now centered especially in Oman and North Africa.
nodes.content:
# Ibadi Islam

## Historical context

Ibadi communities emerged from early disputes about righteous leadership and communal judgment. Historians connect their formation to moderate currents that separated from more militant Kharijites, but Ibadis reject the use of “Kharijite” as a sufficient self-description. Ibadi imamates and scholarly networks developed in Oman, North Africa, and parts of East Africa; communities remain in Oman, Algeria, Libya, Tunisia, and Zanzibar.

## Distinctives and comparative notes

Ibadi thought teaches that an imam should be selected for knowledge and righteousness rather than hereditary lineage and may be removed for grave failure. Its law, hadith transmission, and theology form an independent tradition while sharing basic worship and scripture with other Muslims. Historical doctrines of affiliation and dissociation are more nuanced than popular portrayals of blanket hostility. Modern Ibadi communities are not continuations of violent extremist Kharijite groups.

nodes.title: Ifá
nodes.summary: A Yorùbá divinatory, ethical, and literary system transmitted through trained specialists and extensive oral corpora.
nodes.content:
# Ifá

## Historical context

Ifá developed within Yorùbá religious worlds and is also practiced in related West African and Atlantic diaspora communities. Trained *babaláwo* and *ìyánífá* interpret configurations associated with the 256 *odù*, drawing on a vast repertoire of verses, narratives, prescriptions, and remembered cases. Transmission is oral and initiatory, although practitioners and scholars have also produced substantial written collections.

## Distinctives and comparative notes

Consultation links a client's circumstances with moral reflection, sacrifice, medicine, and relations among humans, òrìṣà, and ancestors. Ifá is more than fortune-telling: its corpus preserves philosophy, history, poetry, and practical reasoning. The branch relation locates it in Yorùbá tradition without reducing every Yorùbá practice to Ifá. Cuban and Brazilian forms have their own languages, institutions, and histories of adaptation.

outbound.title: Yorùbá Religion
outbound.citation: William Bascom, Ifa Divination (1969)

nodes.title: Iglesia ni Cristo
nodes.summary: A Filipino Christian restorationist church founded by Felix Y. Manalo and known internationally by its Tagalog name.
nodes.content:
# Iglesia ni Cristo

## Historical development

Felix Y. Manalo registered Iglesia ni Cristo with the Philippine government in 1914 after engagement with several Protestant and restorationist currents. The church expanded from Manila through centralized administration, purpose-built congregations, disciplined lay participation, and overseas communities serving the Filipino diaspora. Leadership has remained in the Manalo family through successive executive ministers.

## Belief and practice

Iglesia ni Cristo teaches that the one God is the Father, that Jesus is the uniquely appointed human Son and Savior, and that the church represents a restoration of the true church. It rejects the Trinity, practices baptism by immersion, and places strong emphasis on worship attendance, unity, evangelism, and centralized authority. Its Tagalog name means “Church of Christ”; it is unrelated institutionally to the Stone-Campbell Churches of Christ.

nodes.title: Inca Imperial Religion
nodes.summary: The state cults and negotiated local religious worlds of Tawantinsuyu in the Andes.
canonicalTexts: Quechua ritual hymns in colonial records
nodes.content:
# Inca Imperial Religion

## Historical context

The Inca state expanded rapidly across Tawantinsuyu during the fifteenth and early sixteenth centuries, organizing royal ancestor cults, solar institutions, pilgrimage centers, estates, and a calendrical ritual economy. It incorporated rather than erased many local Andean powers and sacred places. Most written descriptions date after Spanish invasion and must be read alongside archaeology, Indigenous-language testimony, and colonial political pressures.

## Distinctives and comparative notes

Inti, Viracocha, royal mummies, *huacas*, mountain beings, reciprocal labor, divination, and offerings connected kin groups with state and landscape. The capacocha sacrifices were exceptional high-level rites, not a summary of daily religion. “Inca religion” should not absorb all Quechua, Aymara, or Andean practice. Contemporary Andean communities sustain distinct relationships with earth, saints, ancestors, and mountains through histories that include but exceed the empire.

nodes.title: Independent Christian Churches and Churches of Christ
nodes.summary: Congregationally independent Stone-Campbell churches occupying a middle stream between Disciples and a cappella Churches of Christ.
nodes.content:
# Independent Christian Churches and Churches of Christ

## Historical development

Independent Christian Churches developed from congregations and institutions that resisted the increasingly denominational structure of the Disciples of Christ during the early and mid-twentieth century. The separation was gradual and was marked by disputes over open membership, missionary agencies, property, and denominational organization. The North American Christian Convention became an important gathering point without governing local churches.

## Organization and practice

These congregations usually practice believer's baptism by immersion, celebrate Communion weekly, use instrumental music, and emphasize local autonomy. Bible colleges and independent mission agencies connect congregations without forming a binding hierarchy. Their name overlaps with the noninstrumental Churches of Christ, but historians normally distinguish the two Stone-Campbell streams by worship practices and institutional histories.

nodes.title: Indigenous American Religions (Comparative)
nodes.summary: A comparative umbrella for the distinct place-based religious traditions of Indigenous peoples across the Americas.
canonicalTexts: Ceremonial, diplomatic, and ecological knowledge corpora
nodes.content:
# Indigenous American Religions (Comparative)

## Historical context

The Americas contain thousands of sovereign peoples with distinct languages, lands, ceremonial systems, and histories. Invasion brought epidemic disease, missionization, dispossession, enslavement, bans on ceremony, boarding schools, and extractive research. Communities nevertheless maintained, renewed, and sometimes strategically concealed religious life while creating new movements under colonial pressure.

## Distinctives and comparative notes

Land, kinship, nonhuman persons, reciprocal obligation, dreams, seasonal ceremony, and oral transmission recur without forming one pan-Indigenous theology. This node is an analytical navigation aid only. Its placement near “animism” marks a debated academic comparison, not a community identity; nation-specific names, sovereignty, and restrictions on sacred knowledge take precedence.

nodes.title: Insight Meditation Movement
nodes.summary: Modern transnational vipassanā networks derived chiefly from Burmese and Theravāda meditation reforms.
nodes.content:
# Insight Meditation Movement

## Historical context

Lay-oriented vipassanā methods expanded in colonial and postcolonial Burma through teachers such as Ledi Sayadaw, Mahasi Sayadaw, and U Ba Khin. Asian and Western students carried related techniques into global retreat centers during the later twentieth century. Distinct lineages use different instructions and should not be collapsed into one standardized method.

## Distinctives and comparative notes

Programs commonly emphasize systematic mindfulness of changing bodily and mental events, intensive retreat, and practical instruction. Some retain chanting, merit, rebirth, and monastic authority; others translate practice into psychological language. Modern accessibility is a real innovation built from Theravāda sources, not proof that meditation was always the principal practice of most Buddhist laypeople.

nodes.title: International Christian Church
nodes.summary: A restorationist church network organized after a split from the International Churches of Christ.
canonicalTexts: International Christian Churches SoldOut Movement Crown of Thorns Project
nodes.content:
# International Christian Church

## Historical development

The International Christian Church coalesced in Portland, Oregon, around Kip McKean and congregations that separated from the International Churches of Christ during the mid-2000s. Its leaders presented the new network as a renewed continuation of the earlier discipling and mission model. Church planting campaigns subsequently established congregations in multiple countries.

## Organization and practice

The movement teaches baptism by immersion for disciples, structured personal discipling, and an obligation to evangelize the world. It maintains a more coordinated global mission program than the decentralized post-2003 International Churches of Christ. The two bodies share close Stone-Campbell ancestry but are institutionally separate and differ over leadership, governance, and the interpretation of their common history.

nodes.title: International Churches of Christ
nodes.summary: A global Stone-Campbell network formed from the Boston Movement within Churches of Christ.
canonicalTexts: International Churches of Christ Unity Proposal
nodes.content:
# International Churches of Christ

## Historical development

The International Churches of Christ developed from a rapidly growing ministry led by Kip McKean in Lexington, Massachusetts, and then Boston from 1979. Its discipling system, missionary expansion, and centralized sector leadership differentiated the Boston Movement from other Churches of Christ. It adopted the International Churches of Christ name in the 1990s and underwent substantial decentralization after a leadership crisis in 2002–2003.

## Organization and practice

Congregations retain Stone-Campbell emphases on the Bible, baptism by immersion, and restoration of early Christian discipleship. Intensive mentoring and a strong expectation of evangelism have been distinctive, although practice changed after public criticism and internal reforms. Present congregations cooperate through regional and international networks rather than the former centralized structure.

nodes.title: International Society for Krishna Consciousness
nodes.summary: A global Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇava movement founded by A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada in New York.
nodes.content:
# International Society for Krishna Consciousness

## Historical context

A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada founded ISKCON in New York in 1966 as a modern institution within Bengali Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇavism. Public chanting, book distribution, temples, communal residences, and vegetarian food programs enabled rapid global growth. After Prabhupada’s death, governance and leadership developed through a collective commission amid reforms and controversies.

## Distinctives and comparative notes

ISKCON centers devotion to Kṛṣṇa through congregational chanting of the Hare Krishna mantra, deity worship, scriptural study, ethical vows, and service. It teaches Caitanya as a divine descent and emphasizes disciplined *bhakti*. Its countercultural Western history is only one chapter of a transnational community now substantially rooted in India and diverse diasporas.

nodes.title: Inuit Religions
nodes.summary: Diverse land-, sea-, kin-, and spirit-centered traditions among Inuit across the circumpolar North.
nodes.content:
# Inuit Religions

## Historical context

Inuit communities extend across Kalaallit Nunaat, Canada, Alaska, and Chukotka, with distinct languages, colonial histories, and local practices. Mission Christianity, forced settlement, residential schooling, relocations, wage economies, and climate disruption have transformed religious life. Early explorers and ethnographers often generalized from one region, so “Inuit religion” must remain a plural comparative category.

## Distinctives and comparative notes

Hunting ethics, naming, human-animal reciprocity, weather, sea powers, helping spirits, storytelling, and the work of ritual specialists appeared in varying forms. Terms such as *angakkuq* belong to specific linguistic contexts and are not universal equivalents of a global “shaman.” Many Inuit communities are strongly Christian while preserving inherited values and practices. Popular fascination with taboos or sea-woman narratives should not eclipse contemporary sovereignty and knowledge governance.

nodes.title: Iranian Zoroastrianism
nodes.summary: The continuous but changing Zoroastrian communities of post-conquest Iran, historically concentrated around Yazd and Kerman.
nodes.content:
# Iranian Zoroastrianism

## Historical formation

Zoroastrian communities persisted in Iran after the Islamic conquests despite legal disadvantage, demographic decline, migration, and periodic persecution. Yazd and Kerman became especially important centers. Exchanges of questions and answers with Parsi priests produced the Persian Rivayats, while nineteenth- and twentieth-century reform, urbanization, and diaspora reshaped communal institutions.

## Community and distinction

Iranian Zoroastrians share scripture, ritual lineages, and modern networks with Parsis but possess distinct language histories, calendars, customs, and social experiences. Older outsider labels can be derogatory and should not replace community self-designations such as Zartoshti. Contemporary Iranian practice includes both priestly ritual continuity and diverse modern reinterpretations.

nodes.title: Islam
nodes.summary: A monotheistic tradition arising in seventh-century Arabia around the Qur'anic revelations proclaimed by Muhammad and the community formed around them.
nodes.content:
# Islam

## Historical genesis

Islam emerged in western Arabia in the early seventh century CE through revelations Muhammad proclaimed as the speech of God. The Qur'an addresses its audience in conversation with Biblical figures, Arabian religious practices, eschatological preaching, and the wider world of Late Antiquity. Muhammad's migration from Mecca to Medina in 622 marks the beginning of the Islamic calendar and the formation of a community with religious, social, and political dimensions.

After Muhammad's death in 632, disputes over leadership and authority contributed to the eventual formation of Sunni, Shi'a, and other currents. Expanding Muslim-ruled societies brought Arabic-speaking believers into sustained contact with Christians, Jews, Zoroastrians, philosophers, and many local traditions. Qur'anic exegesis, hadith criticism, jurisprudence, theology, philosophy, and Sufism developed distinct methods for negotiating revelation, reason, and inherited practice.

## Ideas and practice

Islam centers the oneness of God (*tawḥīd*), prophecy, revelation, moral accountability, and resurrection. The Qur'an presents Abraham, Moses, Jesus, and other figures as participants in a history of divine guidance while asserting its own corrective and confirmatory role. Common practices include profession of faith, ritual prayer, almsgiving, Ramadan fasting, and pilgrimage to Mecca, though lived expressions vary greatly across societies.

## Comparative notes

The graph's influence edges indicate a shared Late Antique repertoire, textual conversation, and historical contact—not a claim that Islam is reducible to “borrowed” Judaism or Christianity. The possible Zoroastrian edge is less certain. Iranian converts and institutions profoundly shaped later Islamic civilization, but assigning particular early doctrines to Zoroastrian sources requires case-by-case evidence and remains disputed.

outbound.citation: Patricia Crone, The Nativist Prophets of Early Islamic Iran (2012)

nodes.title: Ismailism
nodes.summary: A Shi'a family recognizing the Imamate through Isma'il ibn Ja'far and known for Fatimid institutions and esoteric interpretation.
nodes.content:
# Ismailism

## Historical context

Ismaili communities emerged from disagreement over succession after Ja'far al-Sadiq in the eighth century. A far-reaching missionary network supported the Fatimid caliphate, founded in North Africa in 909 and later centered in Cairo. Further succession disputes produced Nizari and Tayyibi Musta'li branches, each developing diasporic institutions and distinct lines of authority.

## Distinctives and comparative notes

Ismaili thought emphasizes the Imam's authoritative guidance and layered interpretation that relates outward practice to inward meaning. Fatimid scholars contributed to philosophy, law, administration, and learning; historical caricatures of secretive “Assassins” distort Nizari life. Ismailism is internally diverse: Nizaris recognize a present living Imam, while Tayyibi communities follow a line of concealed Imams represented through missionary leadership. It shares Shi'a devotion to the Prophet's family without following the Twelver succession.

nodes.title: iTaukei Fijian Religious Traditions
nodes.summary: Indigenous Fijian traditions of ancestors, vanua, chiefly authority, land and sea, exchange, spirit powers, and indigenized Christianity.
nodes.content:
# iTaukei Fijian Religious Traditions

## Historical context

Fiji’s islands developed varied chiefdoms and ritual systems through local histories and exchange with Tonga and other Pacific societies. Nineteenth-century warfare, Methodist conversion, colonial government, and the formation of modern chiefly institutions transformed religious authority. Christianity is now integral to much iTaukei communal life, while ancestral and *vanua* responsibilities continue in changing forms.

## Distinctives and comparative notes

The *vanua* joins land, people, chiefly order, ancestors, and collective obligation rather than naming land as a detachable commodity. Ceremonial exchange, yaqona, *meke*, funerals, and church life can all enact sacred relationship. “Melanesian” is a geographic-comparative placement; Fiji also has strong Polynesian connections and should not be forced into a single cultural block.

nodes.title: Jainism
nodes.summary: An Indian tradition centered on the Jinas' path of nonviolence, karmic purification, disciplined knowledge, and liberation.
nodes.content:
# Jainism

## Historical context

Jain communities trace a succession of twenty-four Jinas, with Pārśva and Mahāvīra historically associated with the eastern Gangetic world before and during early Buddhism. Monastic and lay networks spread across India, supported literary cultures in Prakrit, Sanskrit, and regional languages, and developed Digambara and Śvetāmbara formations.

## Distinctives and comparative notes

Jain teaching describes living souls bound by karmic matter and liberated through right faith, knowledge, conduct, and severe nonviolence. Ascetics model renunciation; laypeople pursue adapted vows, generosity, pilgrimage, and temple or non-image-based worship. Jainism shares karma and rebirth vocabulary with Buddhist and Hindu traditions but offers a distinct pluralist ontology and should not be treated as a branch of either.

nodes.title: Japanese Confucian Traditions
nodes.summary: Japanese traditions of Confucian learning, ethics, ritual, and political thought, especially diverse and influential in the Tokugawa period.
nodes.content:
# Japanese Confucian Traditions

## Historical context

Confucian learning entered Japan with writing, Buddhism, and continental statecraft, but expanded dramatically under Tokugawa rule. Thinkers including Hayashi Razan, Itō Jinsai, Ogyū Sorai, and Kaibara Ekken debated Zhu Xi orthodoxy, ancient texts, language, and practical ethics. Schools served domains, townspeople, and private academies while interacting with Buddhist and kami traditions.

## Distinctives and comparative notes

Japanese Confucianism shaped education, household ethics, political argument, and ideals of cultivation without becoming a single legally bounded denomination. Some teachers emphasized metaphysics, others philology, ritual, or empirical learning. Modern claims that it supplied a timeless national morality overlook conflict among schools and the selective reuse of Confucian concepts by Meiji and later institutions.

nodes.title: Jediism
nodes.summary: A decentralized set of spiritual and ethical movements adapting Jedi imagery and the Force from Star Wars into lived practice.
canonicalTexts: Star Wars films and related media
Temple of the Jedi Order doctrine
nodes.content:
# Jediism

## Historical context

Jedi identification appeared among fans and online communities in the late twentieth century, then gained visibility through religion responses in several national censuses beginning in 2001. Organizations developed training programs, ethical codes, clergy roles, and meditation practices with varying degrees of seriousness and relation to fandom.

## Distinctives and comparative notes

Jediists commonly interpret the Force as a spiritual, ethical, psychological, or metaphorical principle and cultivate service, self-discipline, and emotional balance. Star Wars itself drew eclectically on Asian religions, monastic imagery, mythology, and film traditions; direct lineage claims to Buddhism or Daoism would therefore be misleading.

nodes.title: Jehovah's Witnesses
nodes.summary: A millenarian Christian-origin movement descending from Charles Taze Russell's Bible Student networks.
canonicalTexts: New World Translation of the Holy Scriptures
nodes.content:
# Jehovah's Witnesses

## Historical context

Charles Taze Russell organized Bible study circles in the 1870s within a wider American millenarian environment. The Watch Tower Society coordinated publishing and preaching, while leadership under Joseph Rutherford reshaped organization and adopted the name Jehovah's Witnesses in 1931. The movement expanded globally despite bans, imprisonment, and legal disputes over conscientious objection and public evangelism.

## Distinctives and comparative notes

Witnesses worship Jehovah as the one God, reject the Trinity, understand Jesus as God's first creation, and expect divine rule to replace present political systems. They avoid blood transfusions, military service, partisan politics, and many holidays, and practice intensive door-to-door or public witnessing. Their Adventist influence was indirect rather than simple denominational descent. Most Nicene churches reject Witness theology, while historical classification recognizes its Christian and Biblical genealogy.

nodes.title: Jeungsanism
nodes.summary: A family of Korean new religions rooted in the teachings attributed to Kang Jeungsan and visions of cosmic renewal.
nodes.content:
# Jeungsanism

## Historical context

Jeungsanist movements arose in Korea around Kang Il-sun, known as Kang Jeungsan, whose followers understood his ritual work and teaching as a response to the crises of the late Joseon and colonial periods. After his death in 1909, several organizations developed distinct successions, scriptures, and institutions; Jeungsanism is therefore a family label rather than one centralized church.

## Distinctives and comparative notes

Jeungsanist traditions commonly anticipate a transformed Later World brought through the resolution of accumulated grievance and the reordering of cosmic relationships. Healing, ethical cultivation, ritual, and reverence for Kang vary by movement. Their vocabulary draws on Korean popular religion, Confucian cosmology, Daoist techniques, Buddhism, and older millenarian currents without reducing cleanly to any one source.

nodes.title: Jinja Shinto
nodes.summary: The postwar field of shrine-centered Shinto ritual, priesthood, festivals, and administration, especially shrines affiliated with Jinja Honchō.
nodes.content:
# Jinja Shinto

## Historical context

After Japan’s 1945 separation of religion and state, shrines formerly embedded in government administration reorganized as private religious corporations. Jinja Honchō, commonly translated as the Association of Shinto Shrines, formed in 1946 and today affiliates many—but not all—shrines. Local shrines retain their own histories, priestly families, kami, parish relations, and festivals.

## Distinctives and comparative notes

Shrine practice centers offerings, purification, prayer, seasonal festivals, amulets, and care for kami tied to places, communities, occupations, or national mythology. “Jinja Shinto” is an institutional and scholarly category, not a creed to which every visitor formally subscribes. It must also be distinguished from prewar State Shinto and from independent Sect Shinto organizations.

nodes.title: Jōdo Shinshū
nodes.summary: The Japanese True Pure Land tradition associated with Shinran, emphasizing entrusting faith and Amitābha’s other-power.
nodes.content:
# Jōdo Shinshū

## Historical context

Shinran, a disciple of Hōnen, interpreted Pure Land teaching around radical dependence on Amitābha’s vow and did not initially establish a formal school. Communities organized around his descendants and writings, eventually developing powerful Honganji institutions and several branches. The tradition later spread through Japanese migration, forming durable communities in the Americas and elsewhere.

## Distinctives and comparative notes

Jōdo Shinshū treats *shinjin*, the entrusting heart-mind given through other-power, as decisive; *nembutsu* expresses gratitude rather than accumulating merit to compel salvation. Its clergy may marry and its temples often function through family and lay participation, challenging simple monastic-versus-lay categories. “Faith Buddhism” can be a helpful comparison, but Christian analogies should not replace its Mahāyāna account of non-self, vow, and awakening.

nodes.title: Jōdo-shū
nodes.summary: A Japanese Pure Land school founded by Hōnen that centers recitation of Amitābha Buddha’s name as the accessible path to birth in Sukhāvatī.
nodes.content:
# Jōdo-shū

## Historical context

Hōnen taught an independent Pure Land path in late Heian and early Kamakura Japan, conventionally dating his school’s founding to 1175. Drawing on Chinese Pure Land masters and Genshin, he selected vocal *nembutsu* as the practice suited to an age of declining Dharma. His diverse disciples formed several lineages; some survived as Jōdo-shū while others contributed to separate movements.

## Distinctives and comparative notes

Jōdo-shū encourages trusting Amitābha’s vow and reciting *Namu Amida Butsu*, alongside ethical conduct, liturgy, memorial practice, and study. Hōnen emphasized the selected practice without necessarily denying all value to other Buddhist disciplines. Differences from Jōdo Shinshū concern interpretation of faith, practice, clerical form, and institutional history, not devotion to a different Buddha or Pure Land canon.

nodes.title: Jogye Order
nodes.summary: The largest modern Korean Buddhist order, grounded in Seon practice and a lineage identity associated with the historical Jogye tradition.
nodes.content:
# Jogye Order

## Historical context

The modern Jogye Order emerged through twentieth-century efforts to unify and reform Korean monastic Buddhism after Japanese colonial rule, while invoking older Seon lineages and the name of China’s Caoxi or Jogye tradition. Its institutional consolidation involved disputes over clerical marriage, property, and the restoration of celibate monastic leadership. It now administers many major temples in South Korea and supports international centers.

## Distinctives and comparative notes

Jogye training gives prominence to *ganhwa Seon*, meditation focused on a critical phrase or *hwadu*, together with Vinaya, chanting, doctrinal education, repentance, and devotional ritual. The order draws heavily on Jinul’s integration of sudden awakening with gradual cultivation. It is not synonymous with all Korean Buddhism: Taego, Cheontae, and other orders preserve distinct institutions and emphases.

nodes.title: John Frum Movement
nodes.summary: An Indigenous prophetic and political movement centered on Tanna in Vanuatu.
canonicalTexts: John Frum song and ritual corpus
nodes.content:
# John Frum Movement

## Historical context

The John Frum movement arose on Tanna under the Anglo-French colonial regime, mission pressure, plantation labor, and debates over local governance. Prophecies and public organization became especially visible around the Second World War and the arrival of American forces. Movement communities have pursued kastom, political autonomy, moral order, and expected transformation through changing historical circumstances.

## Distinctives and comparative notes

Friday observance, songs, marching, village organization, volcanic and ancestral landscapes, and narratives of John Frum vary among adherents. Outsiders often reduce the movement to naïve expectation of manufactured “cargo,” ignoring its anticolonial analysis and enduring institutions. The branch relation uses a familiar scholarly category for navigation, while the parent node explains why “cargo cult” is contested and cannot exhaust Tannese meanings.

nodes.title: Jonang
nodes.summary: A Tibetan Buddhist tradition known for Kālacakra practice and a distinctive other-emptiness interpretation.
nodes.content:
# Jonang

## Historical context

Jonang institutions developed in Tibet from the thirteenth century, with Dolpopa Sherab Gyaltsen and Tāranātha among their major authors. Seventeenth-century political changes converted many central Tibetan monasteries to Gelug control, leading outsiders to presume the school extinct. Jonang communities nevertheless continued in eastern Tibet and have gained wider recognition in recent decades.

## Distinctives and comparative notes

Jonang preserves a complete Kālacakra system and teaches *shentong*, or “other-emptiness,” describing ultimate awakened qualities as empty of adventitious defilement rather than empty of their own nature. Critics and Jonang authors interpret this language differently. The debate belongs within Tibetan Madhyamaka and buddha-nature discourse, not a simple contrast between belief and nihilism.

nodes.title: Judaism
nodes.summary: An evolving monotheistic tradition rooted in ancient Israelite religion, covenantal law, textual interpretation, and communal practice.
nodes.content:
# Judaism

## Historical genesis

Judaism developed from the religions of ancient Israel and Judah rather than appearing at a single founding moment. The Hebrew Bible preserves memories of mobile pastoral communities, monarchy, temple sacrifice, prophetic criticism, conquest, exile, and restoration. Archaeology and textual study indicate a long movement from a West Semitic religious environment toward the exclusive worship of YHWH. The Babylonian exile in the sixth century BCE and the Persian-period restoration were especially important for the formation, collection, and interpretation of authoritative texts.

The destruction of the Second Temple in 70 CE did not simply end one religion and begin another. Diverse Jewish groups had already organized life through scripture, prayer, legal interpretation, pilgrimage, sacrifice, and local assemblies in different proportions. Rabbinic Judaism gradually became a particularly influential framework through the Mishnah, the Palestinian and Babylonian Talmuds, and later legal and philosophical traditions. Karaite, Samaritan, mystical, and other Jewish communities complicate any single linear genealogy.

## Ideas and practice

The covenant between God and Israel, Torah, ethical obligation, sacred time, collective memory, and argument over interpretation are central themes. Jewish thought ranges from apophatic philosophy to Kabbalistic accounts of divine emanation, and from strict naturalism to robust messianic expectation. Practice is equally important: Sabbath, festivals, dietary rules, prayer, study, charity, and life-cycle observances make tradition tangible in community.

## Comparative notes

Some scholars argue that Persian-period contact with Zoroastrian traditions sharpened Jewish ideas about angels, resurrection, final judgment, and cosmic opposition. Contact is historically plausible, but the direction and scale of transmission remain debated; related ideas may also reflect internal development or a wider West Asian environment. OpenGrail therefore marks that edge as **minority scholarly**, not as a settled claim of direct borrowing.

nodes.title: Kabbalah
nodes.summary: A family of Jewish esoteric traditions concerning divine manifestation, creation, scripture, ritual intention, and restoration.
nodes.content:
# Kabbalah

## Historical context

Earlier Jewish mystical and cosmological writings preceded Kabbalah, but recognizable schools emerged in medieval Provence and Iberia. The *Zohar*, composed largely in thirteenth-century Castile, became foundational. After the expulsion from Spain, Safed teachers such as Moses Cordovero and Isaac Luria developed influential systems that spread through prayer, ethics, messianism, and later Hasidism.

## Distinctives and comparative notes

Kabbalists interpret Torah through symbolic structures including the ten *sefirot*, which describe dynamic divine manifestation without simply multiplying gods. Lurianic traditions discuss contraction, shattered vessels, and restoration through commandments performed with intention. Kabbalah is an internal Jewish current grounded in rabbinic practice, though Christian Kabbalah and occult movements later adapted selected symbols. Popular numerology alone does not represent its full textual and ritual discipline.

nodes.title: Kagyu
nodes.summary: A family of Tibetan Buddhist transmission lineages associated with Marpa, Milarepa, Gampopa, Mahāmudrā, and yogic practice.
nodes.content:
# Kagyu

## Historical context

Kagyu traditions arose from Tibetan reception of Indian tantric transmissions, remembered through the teacher sequence Tilopa, Nāropa, Marpa, Milarepa, and Gampopa. Gampopa joined yogic instruction with Kadam monastic path teaching. Multiple “major” and “minor” Kagyu branches followed; Karma Kagyu became especially prominent through the Karmapa incarnation lineage.

## Distinctives and comparative notes

Mahāmudrā meditation and the Six Dharmas of Nāropa are characteristic, alongside monastic study, ritual, and bodhisattva training. Popular images of Kagyu as purely experiential can obscure its substantial textual and institutional learning. Lineage histories authorize practice but are not simple organizational charts: teachers exchanged instructions across Tibetan schools, and sublineages frequently overlap.

nodes.title: Kālīkula
nodes.summary: A family of Śākta traditions oriented toward Kālī and related fierce goddesses, especially influential in eastern India.
nodes.content:
# Kālīkula

## Historical context

Kālīkula denotes Goddess lineages in which Kālī and related deities occupy the central place. Tantric sources, temple cults, vernacular poetry, and household devotion made these traditions especially influential in Bengal, Assam, Odisha, and neighboring regions.

## Distinctives and comparative notes

Kālī may be approached as terrifying time, protective mother, liberating wisdom, or supreme reality. Practice ranges from public festival and domestic worship to restricted initiatory ritual. Kālīkula overlaps with other Śākta and Śaiva systems, and the umbrella label should not erase differences among regional goddesses and lineages.

nodes.title: Karaite Judaism
nodes.summary: A Jewish tradition prioritizing the Hebrew Bible and rejecting the Talmud as divinely binding oral Torah.
nodes.content:
# Karaite Judaism

## Historical context

Karaite movements became visible under the early Islamic caliphates, with important centers in Iraq, Jerusalem, Byzantium, Crimea, and Egypt. Their origins involved multiple scripturalist currents rather than a single uncontested founder. Medieval Karaite scholars produced major works of Hebrew grammar, exegesis, law, and calendar calculation while debating Rabbanite contemporaries. Communities survive principally in Israel and diaspora settings.

## Distinctives and comparative notes

Karaites regard the Tanakh as revelation and require interpreters to derive practice from its text rather than accept the rabbinic oral law as intrinsically authoritative. They nonetheless possess inherited interpretive traditions and communal rulings, so “Bible only” can oversimplify their method. Practices concerning calendar, Sabbath, dietary law, and fringes may differ from Rabbanite norms. Karaite identity is fully Jewish and should not be confused with Protestant scripturalism merely because both criticize extra-scriptural authority.

nodes.title: Karma Kagyu
nodes.summary: A major Kagyu lineage founded by Düsum Khyenpa and led through the successive reincarnation line of the Karmapas.
nodes.content:
# Karma Kagyu

## Historical context

Karma Kagyu, also called Karma Kamtsang, traces its Tibetan institutional formation to Düsum Khyenpa, the First Karmapa, a student of Gampopa. Successive Karmapas and associated lineage holders developed monasteries, textual traditions, artistic patronage, and retreat systems across Tibet and the Himalayas. Following exile, teachers established substantial international networks; rival recognitions of the seventeenth Karmapa have affected contemporary institutions.

## Distinctives and comparative notes

The lineage is especially associated with Mahāmudrā, the Six Dharmas of Nāropa, guru yoga, and the continuity of oral instruction within a shared Tibetan Buddhist curriculum. Its Karmapa institution is an early and influential reincarnate-lama succession. Disagreements over recognition should be described without declaring one claimant spiritually valid, and Karma Kagyu should not be treated as synonymous with every Kagyu branch.

nodes.title: Kashmir Śaivism
nodes.summary: A family of nondual tantric Śaiva systems developed in Kashmir, including Trika and Pratyabhijñā.
nodes.content:
# Kashmir Śaivism

## Historical context

Between roughly the eighth and twelfth centuries, Kashmiri authors developed sophisticated Śaiva tantric philosophies and ritual systems. Somānanda, Utpaladeva, Abhinavagupta, and Kṣemarāja are especially influential. Modern usage groups related but distinct currents—Trika, Krama, Spanda, and Pratyabhijñā—under one convenient label.

## Distinctives and comparative notes

These systems often identify ultimate reality with self-aware Śiva-consciousness whose free power manifests the universe. Liberation is recognition of one's identity with that consciousness, cultivated through initiation, contemplation, ritual, and insight. The modern global presentation as a single “Kashmir Shaivism” school can obscure historical differences among texts and lineages.

nodes.title: Kemetism
nodes.summary: Modern religious movements reconstructing and renewing devotion to ancient Egyptian deities and concepts.
canonicalTexts: Ancient Egyptian temple and funerary texts
nodes.content:
# Kemetism

## Historical context

Kemetism includes modern movements that revive or reconstruct religions of ancient Egypt, with organized communities developing especially from the 1970s onward. Practitioners use Egyptology, translated texts, museum collections, personal devotion, and new ritual composition. Kemetic Orthodoxy, independent reconstructionists, and groups linking Egypt to African diaspora identity differ significantly in authority, theology, and cultural framing.

## Distinctives and comparative notes

Devotion to Netjeru, offerings, shrine practice, ancestor reverence, and ethical commitment to *ma'at* commonly appear. Modern life lacks the ancient temple economy and divine kingship, so all revival involves selection and adaptation. The branch relation denotes intentional historical reception, not unbroken priestly succession. Responsible practice also navigates colonial histories of Egyptology and debates over Egypt's African and Mediterranean identities.

nodes.title: Khalsa
nodes.summary: The initiated Sikh collective founded by Guru Gobind Singh, marked by shared discipline, symbols, courage, and corporate authority.
nodes.content:
# Khalsa

## Historical context

Guru Gobind Singh inaugurated the Khalsa at Anandpur in 1699 through initiation with *amrit*, amid conflict and community consolidation. Initiates adopted the names Singh or Kaur and a shared discipline. Eighteenth-century Khalsa bands, later Sikh polities, colonial military categories, and modern reform all shaped its public form.

## Distinctives and comparative notes

The Khalsa ideal joins devotion with readiness to defend justice and the vulnerable. Initiated Sikhs maintain the five Ks and a code governing worship, conduct, and communal responsibility. Not all Sikhs are formally initiated, but the Khalsa profoundly shapes Sikh identity. Reducing it to a warrior order misses its devotional, ethical, and egalitarian dimensions.

nodes.title: Khurramism
nodes.summary: An umbrella for early Islamic-era Iranian religious and revolutionary movements known chiefly through hostile external accounts.
nodes.content:
# Khurramism

## Historical setting

Medieval Muslim authors used labels related to *Khurramiyya* for several Iranian movements, most famously the rebellion led by Babak Khorramdin against the Abbasids in the ninth century. Reports attribute distinctive ritual, communal, and reincarnation beliefs, but nearly all detailed descriptions come from opponents. Regional movements grouped under the name may not have shared one organization or theology.

## Scope and interpretation

Scholars often connect Khurramite movements with Mazdakite legacies and older Iranian religious patterns, yet the evidence does not establish simple institutional descent. The branch link therefore carries minority-scholarly certainty. Political revolt, local identity, Islamic-era vocabulary, and inherited cosmologies all likely contributed to a phenomenon reconstructed through highly polemical sources.

nodes.title: Kongo Religious Traditions
nodes.summary: Religious traditions of Kongo-speaking peoples centered on ancestors, territorial powers, healing, moral order, and traffic between visible and invisible worlds.
nodes.content:
# Kongo Religious Traditions

## Historical context

Kongo-speaking societies developed across the lower Congo region before the Kingdom of Kongo’s encounter with Portuguese Christianity in the late fifteenth century. Courts and communities adopted, translated, and contested Christian symbols within existing ideas of sacred authority. Colonial borders, missions, warfare, urbanization, and prophetic movements produced substantial regional variation.

## Distinctives and comparative notes

Kongo cosmologies often distinguish yet connect the lands of living and dead through water, burial, lineage, and cyclical imagery. Specialists work with *minkisi*, empowered assemblages used for healing, protection, oath, or justice. Outsider collections frequently called these objects “fetishes,” a misleading term that detaches them from authorized persons, ingredients, speech, and social obligations.

nodes.title: Konkōkyō
nodes.summary: A Japanese Sect Shinto tradition founded through Konkō Daijin’s revelations and centered on mediation with Tenchi Kane no Kami.
nodes.content:
# Konkōkyō

## Historical context

Farmer Kawate Bunjirō, later known as Konkō Daijin, understood a series of experiences culminating in 1859 as a call from Tenchi Kane no Kami to serve people through spiritual mediation. A network of worship halls grew around his teaching and was recognized within the Meiji Sect Shinto system. Communities later spread beyond Japan, especially through migration.

## Distinctives and comparative notes

Konkōkyō teaches a mutually dependent relationship between the divine parent of the universe and human beings, gratitude amid ordinary life, and *toritsugi*, mediation through listening and counsel. It lacks a rigid conversion boundary and draws on the ritual world of Japanese kami while developing a distinct revealed theology. Its historical legal classification does not reduce it to state shrine practice.

nodes.title: Korean Confucian Traditions
nodes.summary: Korean adaptations of Confucian ethics, ritual, statecraft, and Neo-Confucian philosophy, especially influential during the Joseon dynasty.
canonicalTexts: Essentials of the Learning of the Sages
nodes.content:
# Korean Confucian Traditions

## Historical context

Confucian texts and institutions reached the Korean peninsula through long exchange with China and entered education and government in the Three Kingdoms and Goryeo periods. Joseon rulers made Neo-Confucian learning central to state examinations, academies, family rites, and political debate. Thinkers such as Yi Hwang and Yi I developed sophisticated positions rather than merely repeating Chinese authorities.

## Distinctives and comparative notes

Korean traditions give exceptional attention to Zhu Xi learning, ritual propriety, filial relationships, and debates over the moral emotions and the relation of principle to material force. Lineage rites and academies shaped social order but also became sites of faction and reform. “Korean Confucianism” is a regional intellectual-ritual field, not a separate church or a description of every Korean’s personal religion.

nodes.title: Korean Shamanic Traditions
nodes.summary: Korean ritual traditions in which spirit specialists mediate among deities, ancestors, misfortune, healing, and communal life.
nodes.content:
# Korean Shamanic Traditions

## Historical context

Ritual specialists commonly called *mudang* have served Korean households and communities through changing kingdoms, Confucian governance, colonial suppression, war, urbanization, and heritage policy. Regional lineages differ: some specialists inherit roles, while others understand initiation through spirit illness and calling. “Muism” is a modern umbrella rather than a single church.

## Distinctives and comparative notes

The *gut* combines offerings, music, dance, costume, narrative, divination, and spirit embodiment to heal, guide the dead, secure fortune, or restore relationships. Ancestors, generals, Buddhist figures, and local gods may share a ritual world. Calling the tradition only superstition reproduces elite polemic; romanticizing it as unchanged antiquity ignores continuing innovation and professional practice.

nodes.title: La Luz del Mundo
nodes.summary: A Mexican restorationist Christian church with apostolic leadership and an international congregational network.
aliases: Iglesia del Dios Vivo, Columna y Apoyo de la Verdad, La Luz del Mundo
nodes.content:
# La Luz del Mundo

## Historical development

Eusebio Joaquín González, known in the movement as Aarón, founded La Luz del Mundo in Guadalajara in 1926. The church grew through missionary activity, strong community institutions, distinctive temples, and leadership successions within the Joaquín family. It now has congregations across Mexico and in international migrant communities.

## Belief and practice

The church teaches restoration of the original Christian church through a living apostle, baptism in the name of Jesus Christ, disciplined congregational life, and non-Trinitarian theology. Annual Holy Supper gatherings are central to communal identity. Its official Spanish name translates as “Church of the Living God, Pillar and Ground of the Truth, The Light of the World.”

nodes.title: Lakota Religion
nodes.summary: Sacred traditions of Lakota communities within the Oceti Sakowin, grounded in kinship, land, and ceremony.
nodes.content:
# Lakota Religion

## Historical context

Lakota religious traditions belong within the wider Oceti Sakowin while retaining community, band, family, and ceremonial distinctions. United States warfare, reservation confinement, boarding schools, bans on ceremony, and loss of the Black Hills inflicted sustained religious violence. Elders and families nevertheless maintained and renewed knowledge. Published accounts, including famous mediated biographies, never replace community authority.

## Distinctives and comparative notes

Mitákuye Oyás'i expresses expansive kinship and obligation rather than a detachable slogan. Prayer, pipe traditions, vision seeking, Sun Dance, sacred songs, and relationships with land and beings require proper preparation and sponsorship. Many Lakota are also Christian or Native American Church members. Commercial “medicine men” and pan-Indian workshops often appropriate ceremonies; careful comparison distinguishes public description from permission to perform.

nodes.title: Lao Buddhism
nodes.summary: The Theravāda traditions of Laos and Lao communities, historically embedded in monasteries, festivals, education, and village ritual.
nodes.content:
# Lao Buddhism

## Historical context

Theravāda institutions became closely associated with the Lan Xang kingdom from the fourteenth century, supported by regional exchanges with Khmer, Lanna, Siamese, and Sri Lankan lineages. Monasteries preserved manuscript culture and provided education alongside ritual services. Colonial administration, revolution, socialist government, migration, and diaspora communities each altered the sangha’s public position without ending its social importance.

## Distinctives and comparative notes

Lao communities cultivate merit through alms, ordination, festivals, funerals, precepts, and devotion to images and relics. The *Vessantara Jātaka* and local manuscript traditions have been especially prominent, while protective rites intersect with respect for territorial and ancestral spirits. Lao Buddhism is closely related to neighboring Thai and Khmer traditions but has its own language, histories, institutions, and political setting.

nodes.title: Latin Church
nodes.summary: The largest Catholic sui iuris church, shaped historically by western Latin Christianity and ordinarily using the Roman Rite.
nodes.content:
# Latin Church

## Historical formation

The Latin Church developed from Christian communities in the western Roman world, with Rome becoming its principal episcopal center. Latin liturgy, canon law, monasticism, scholastic theology, and missionary institutions gave western Catholicism a recognizable form. The Roman Rite became overwhelmingly predominant, although Ambrosian, Mozarabic, and several religious-order usages also survived.

## Church, not merely a rite

The Latin Church is a self-governing *sui iuris* church within the Catholic communion, not a synonym for all Catholicism. “Roman Rite” names its largest liturgical tradition, whereas “Latin Church” names the church that ordinarily celebrates it. Eastern Catholic churches share communion with the pope but retain distinct hierarchies, rites, disciplines, and theological inheritances.

nodes.title: Latter Day Saint Fundamentalism
nodes.summary: An umbrella for movements preserving plural marriage and other nineteenth-century Latter Day Saint teachings after institutional discontinuation.
nodes.content:
# Latter Day Saint Fundamentalism

## Historical development

Latter Day Saint fundamentalism arose after the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints ended authorization of new plural marriages around the turn of the twentieth century. Networks of believers maintained that plural marriage and related teachings remained divinely required. These networks later formed several churches, priesthood councils, and independent communities, with no single organization representing all adherents.

## Classification and practice

Fundamentalist groups commonly accept nineteenth-century Latter Day Saint scriptures and temple theology while disputing later institutional changes. Their leadership systems, communal arrangements, and marriage practices differ widely. The historical term “Mormon fundamentalism” remains common in scholarship, but “Latter Day Saint fundamentalism” better distinguishes this diverse family from the contemporary church that formally rejects and excommunicates members for entering plural marriages.

outbound.title: The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints

nodes.title: Latter Day Saint Movement
nodes.summary: A restorationist Christian-origin movement founded by Joseph Smith and continued in several churches with additional scriptures.
nodes.content:
# Latter Day Saint Movement

## Historical context

Joseph Smith organized the Church of Christ in 1830 after publishing the Book of Mormon and reporting visions and angelic mediation. Gathering, temple building, persecution, migration, and Smith's death in 1844 produced a succession crisis. The largest body moved west under Brigham Young and became the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints; Community of Christ and other churches followed different lines.

## Distinctives and comparative notes

Latter Day Saint traditions teach modern revelation, restoration of priesthood authority, covenant ordinances, and an expansive sacred history. Their views of God, premortal existence, scripture, and human exaltation differ from Nicene Christianity. Scholars classify the movement historically within the Christian restorationist environment, while many churches contest its theological Christian status. The graph's branch edge is genealogical and descriptive, not a ruling on confessional boundaries.

nodes.title: Liṅgāyat Tradition
nodes.summary: A Kannada-speaking devotional community centered on Śiva as the personal iṣṭaliṅga and the vachana heritage.
nodes.content:
# Liṅgāyat Tradition

## Historical context

Liṅgāyat or Vīraśaiva community formation is strongly associated with twelfth-century Karnataka and the *vachanas* of Basava, Allama Prabhu, Akka Mahadevi, and other *śaraṇas*. Older Vīraśaiva materials and later institutions complicate any single-founder narrative. Monastic networks and lay communities became enduring features of regional life.

## Distinctives and comparative notes

Initiates wear and worship a personal *iṣṭaliṅga*, emphasizing direct relation to Śiva, work, ethical community, and remembrance. Early vachanas sharply criticized caste hierarchy, gender restrictions, and empty ritual, although historical communities developed varied social arrangements. Whether Liṅgāyatism is categorized as a Hindu denomination or a distinct religion is a modern legal and identity debate; the graph’s Śaiva lineage link is historical, not a verdict on contemporary self-definition.

nodes.title: Lingbao Daoism
nodes.summary: A medieval Daoist scriptural and ritual tradition that systematized universal salvation, liturgy, cosmology, and communal offerings.
canonicalTexts: Five Talismans of the Numinous Treasure
nodes.content:
# Lingbao Daoism

## Historical context

Lingbao scriptures appeared in southern China around the turn of the fifth century, partly associated with Ge Chaofu and earlier Ge-family materials. They combined Celestial Master ritual, Shangqing cosmology, older talismanic traditions, and creatively adapted Buddhist ideas. Lingbao liturgies became central to medieval Daoist communal worship and strongly shaped later ritual repertoires.

## Distinctives and comparative notes

The corpus presents a universal sacred order, elaborate heavens, cycles of cosmic renewal, rites for both living and dead, and salvation extending beyond a narrow initiatory elite. Borrowed Buddhist vocabulary was reworked within Daoist cosmology rather than simply copied. As with Shangqing, Lingbao is best mapped as a historically layered textual-ritual current whose elements persist inside later institutions.

nodes.title: Linji Chan
nodes.summary: A major Chinese Chan lineage associated with Linji Yixuan and later transmission traditions throughout East Asia.
nodes.content:
# Linji Chan

## Historical context

The lineage takes its name from Linji Yixuan, a ninth-century teacher remembered through a later compiled record of sermons and encounters. During the Song dynasty, Linji transmission houses became institutionally dominant and developed influential kōan collections and lineage histories. Monks carried related transmissions to Korea, Vietnam, and Japan, where the Japanese Rinzai name uses another reading of the same characters.

## Distinctives and comparative notes

Linji literature favors abrupt exchanges, shouts, paradoxical language, and criticism of attachment to religious status, while its monasteries also maintained ritual, discipline, study, and seated meditation. Later teachers organized encounter stories into curricula for contemplation and commentary. The dramatic rhetoric should not be mistaken for hostility to all scripture, nor should every lineage descended from Linji be assumed to use identical kōan methods.

nodes.title: Living Church of God
nodes.summary: An Armstrongist denomination formed under Roderick C. Meredith after divisions among Worldwide Church of God successors.
canonicalTexts: Living Church of God Official Statement of Fundamental Beliefs
nodes.content:
# Living Church of God

## Historical development

Roderick C. Meredith organized the Global Church of God after leaving the Worldwide Church of God in 1992. A governance conflict in that body led Meredith and supporters to form the Living Church of God in 1998. The denomination continued international broadcasting, publishing, congregational worship, and observance of biblical festivals.

## Belief and practice

The church teaches seventh-day Sabbath observance, annual holy days, conditional immortality, non-Trinitarian theology, and a future kingdom of God on earth. Its governmental model emphasizes hierarchical ministerial authority. Though sharing Armstrongist ancestry with the United Church of God and other bodies, it is an independent denomination with its own leadership and institutions.

nodes.title: Longmen Daoism
nodes.summary: The most widespread Quanzhen ordination lineage, consolidated in the late imperial period around monastic precepts and internal cultivation.
nodes.content:
# Longmen Daoism

## Historical context

Longmen genealogies trace the lineage to Qiu Chuji, a leading disciple in early Quanzhen, but its durable institutional form emerged much later. Wang Changyue’s seventeenth-century public ordinations at the White Cloud Monastery helped standardize precepts and spread Longmen affiliations across China. Numerous local sublineages subsequently claimed the name with varying relationships to central monasteries.

## Distinctives and comparative notes

Longmen transmission combines celibate monastic identity, ethical precepts, liturgy, meditation, and internal alchemy. The lineage’s broad reach makes it internally diverse; affiliation may record ordination genealogy rather than a uniform contemplative method. Presenting it as an unchanged medieval order would confuse retrospective ancestry with the historically documented expansion of late imperial institutions.

nodes.title: Lu–Wang Confucianism
nodes.summary: A Neo-Confucian current associated with Lu Jiuyuan and Wang Yangming that locates moral principle in the heart-mind and innate knowing.
nodes.content:
# Lu–Wang Confucianism

## Historical context

Lu Jiuyuan challenged approaches he considered overly dependent on external textual investigation, arguing that the moral mind already participates in universal principle. Ming thinker Wang Yangming renewed and expanded this current after a transformative experience in exile. His teachings spread through academies and disciples in China, Japan, Korea, and Vietnam, often provoking orthodox criticism.

## Distinctives and comparative notes

Lu–Wang teaching emphasizes the unity of knowledge and action, recovery of innate moral awareness, and disciplined attention to selfish obstruction. “Innate knowing” does not mean acting on every spontaneous preference; it requires ethical cultivation and correction in concrete affairs. Comparisons with Chan are historically relevant because critics and practitioners recognized shared vocabulary, yet the school frames awakening through Confucian relationships and public responsibility.

nodes.title: Lucumí / Regla de Ocha
nodes.summary: An Afro-Cuban religion joining Yorùbá-derived òrìṣà devotion with Cuban, Catholic, and diaspora histories.
nodes.content:
# Lucumí / Regla de Ocha

## Historical context

Lucumí, also widely called Santería or Regla de Ocha, took shape in colonial and postcolonial Cuba among Yorùbá-speaking captives and descendants, in interaction with other African nations, Catholic institutions, Spiritism, and Cuban social life. Cabildos, ritual houses, kinship, migration, and later transnational networks sustained distinct lineages. Many practitioners prefer Lucumí or Ocha because “Santería” began as an outsider label.

## Distinctives and comparative notes

Initiation, divination, drumming, sacrifice, spirit possession, and reciprocal service to the *oricha* organize practice. Catholic saints may correspond to oricha in historically layered ways, but the beings are not simply identical. Lucumí retains Yorùbá language and concepts while possessing its own Cuban canon of ritual precedent. It should be compared with, not collapsed into, Brazilian Candomblé or contemporary Yorùbá religion.
