Unlike Eleusis, initiation was not restricted by Athenian civic structures, and protection at sea became one celebrated benefit.

## Scope and interpretation

Secrecy obscures ritual detail and even the stable identities of the “Great Gods.” Ancient writers compared them with Cabeiri and other divine groups, but local names and functions should not be harmonized too quickly. The mysteries formed a distinctive sanctuary institution, not a separate doctrine replacing participants’ civic or household worship.

nodes.title: San Religious Traditions (Comparative)
nodes.summary: An analytical umbrella for distinct religious traditions among San peoples of southern Africa, including healing dances, stories, and relations with animals and land.
nodes.content:
# San Religious Traditions (Comparative)

## Historical context

“San” covers peoples with different languages and histories across southern Africa. Pastoral expansion, settler violence, dispossession, labor systems, conservation policy, and mission Christianity profoundly disrupted communities. Ethnographic archives and rock art preserve important evidence but were often collected under unequal conditions and must be interpreted with living communities rather than treated as ownerless data.

## Distinctives and comparative notes

In several documented traditions, communal dances generate healing potency, alter consciousness, and repair relationships; stories connect animals, persons, weather, and ancestral time. These patterns are not universal across every San group. The comparative term “shamanism” can illuminate trance healing but can also import a Siberian model, so the graph marks it as a debated parallel rather than a self-description.

nodes.title: Sarvāstivāda
nodes.summary: A major early Buddhist scholastic and monastic tradition influential in northwestern India and Central Asia.
nodes.content:
# Sarvāstivāda

## Historical context

Sarvāstivāda monastic and scholastic centers flourished across northern India, Kashmir, Gandhāra, and Central Asia. The Vaibhāṣika synthesis associated with the *Mahāvibhāṣā* developed one of Buddhism’s most detailed Abhidharma systems. Many texts survive through Chinese and Tibetan translation, while related Mūlasarvāstivāda discipline continues in Tibetan ordination.

## Distinctives and comparative notes

The school is named for the thesis that conditioned factors in past, present, and future “exist,” a claim designed to explain karma, memory, and temporal continuity without a permanent self. Internal interpretations differed, and critics such as Vasubandhu sharpened later Buddhist philosophy. Sarvāstivāda is institutionally extinct, but its categories remain deeply embedded in East Asian and Tibetan scholastic curricula.

nodes.title: Sasanian Zoroastrianism
nodes.summary: The institutionally elaborated forms of Zoroastrianism under the Sasanian Empire, known through inscriptions and later Middle Persian literature.
nodes.content:
# Sasanian Zoroastrianism

## Historical setting

Sasanian rulers patronized fire temples and priestly institutions while presenting kingship as protected by the gods. Inscriptions of Kerdir document clerical power and competition, but state, court, and local religious life were never perfectly uniform. Avestan transmission and Middle Persian exegesis flourished across this period and after the Islamic conquest.

## Scope and interpretation

Many detailed Zoroastrian cosmological and legal works survive in later manuscripts, so dating particular teachings requires care. “State church” can overstate centralized control across four centuries and a diverse empire. Sasanian tradition was formative for later communities, but it should not be projected unchanged backward onto Zarathustra or Achaemenid Iran.

nodes.title: Satmar Hasidism
nodes.summary: A large Hungarian-rooted Hasidic dynasty known for strict communal institutions and theological anti-Zionism.
nodes.content:
# Satmar Hasidism

## Historical development

Joel Teitelbaum established the Satmar dynasty in Satu Mare, then within Hungary, in the early twentieth century. After surviving the Holocaust he rebuilt the community in New York, where it developed extensive schools, charities, congregations, and Yiddish-speaking neighborhoods. A later succession dispute produced two major leadership centers.

## Teaching and practice

Satmar combines Hasidic devotion with strict halakhic observance, communal separation, and preservation of Yiddish culture. Its influential anti-Zionism argues that Jewish sovereignty before messianic redemption violates traditional prohibitions; this position is theological and differs from secular political anti-Zionism. Satmar is one Hasidic dynasty and does not represent all Haredi Jews.

nodes.title: Sautrāntika
nodes.summary: A historical label for Buddhist Abhidharma critics who privileged sūtra reasoning and developed influential theories of perception and momentariness.
nodes.content:
# Sautrāntika

## Historical context

Later Buddhist doxographies use “Sautrāntika” for teachers who challenged Vaibhāṣika Sarvāstivāda orthodoxy and appealed to sūtras over certain Abhidharma claims. Scholars debate whether this was one organized school, several currents, or a retrospective philosophical category.

## Distinctives and comparative notes

Positions associated with Sautrāntikas include representational theories of perception, seeds or latent continuities, and denial that past and future phenomena exist in the same way as present ones. Their arguments shaped Yogācāra and Buddhist logic. The minority tier flags uncertainty about institutional unity, not the existence of the recorded debates.

nodes.title: Scientology
nodes.summary: A modern religious movement founded by L. Ron Hubbard around auditing, spiritual rehabilitation, and the immortal thetan.
nodes.content:
# Scientology

## Historical context

L. Ron Hubbard introduced Dianetics in 1950 as a therapeutic system and soon reframed it within Scientology, organized through churches from the mid-1950s. The movement spread internationally through courses, missions, celebrity programs, and tightly managed institutions. It has also generated legal conflict, former-member testimony, state scrutiny, and sustained debate over religion, commerce, and organizational control.

## Distinctives and comparative notes

Scientology teaches that the person is an immortal *thetan* whose capacities are constrained by traumatic impressions and a vast spiritual history. Auditing with an E-meter and progressive training seek increasing freedom. Academic description of these beliefs does not validate therapeutic or scientific claims. Legal recognition differs by country, and analysis should distinguish the religion's theology from evidence-based mental-health care.

nodes.title: Second Temple Judaism
nodes.summary: The diverse Jewish institutions, texts, practices, and movements of the restored Temple era through 70 CE.
nodes.content:
# Second Temple Judaism

## Historical context

Second Temple Judaism spans Persian, Hellenistic, Hasmonean, and Roman rule from the Temple's restoration to its destruction in 70 CE. Jerusalem sacrifice remained a major focus, but diaspora communities, synagogues, scripture, pilgrimage, legal interpretation, and apocalyptic hope created many forms of Jewish life. Pharisees, Sadducees, Essenes, Jesus movements, revolutionaries, and Jews outside named parties shared some practices while disputing others.

## Distinctives and comparative notes

There was no single Second Temple orthodoxy. Communities differed over calendars, purity, resurrection, priesthood, foreign rule, and which writings carried special authority. The period supplied the immediate matrix for both rabbinic Judaism and Christianity, but neither can be projected backward as its inevitable outcome. “Late Judaism,” once common in older scholarship, misleadingly treats a creative era as merely transitional.

nodes.title: Sect Shinto
nodes.summary: A modern administrative category for diverse Japanese religious organizations recognized separately from state-administered shrines.
canonicalTexts: Founders' teachings of the thirteen recognized sects
nodes.content:
# Sect Shinto

## Historical context

Meiji authorities classified thirteen organizations as Sect Shinto, including mountain-worship, purification, healing, and revival movements. Some drew on older confraternities; others formed around charismatic founders. The category distinguished them from government-administered shrines and subjected them to the legal framework for religious teaching organizations.

## Distinctives and comparative notes

The recognized sects never shared one theology: they venerated different kami, mountains, founders, and ritual disciplines. “Sect Shinto” is therefore best understood as a historical legal umbrella, not a coherent denomination. Some later movements, including Tenrikyo, passed through related classification while developing strong independent identities. Modern descendants may prefer their own names and histories to the inherited category.

nodes.title: Secular Buddhism
nodes.summary: Modern Buddhist-inspired approaches that bracket or reinterpret cosmology while emphasizing ethics, practice, and human flourishing.
nodes.content:
# Secular Buddhism

## Historical context

Secular Buddhist networks emerged prominently in Europe, North America, and Australasia from late twentieth-century convert Buddhism, mindfulness culture, historical-critical study, and humanist ethics. Writers and communities differ substantially, so the label describes a family of experiments rather than an institution with a common creed.

## Distinctives and comparative notes

Many participants treat rebirth, karma across lives, supernatural beings, and cosmology as optional, symbolic, or historically conditioned while retaining meditation, ethical precepts, community, and dependent arising. Critics argue that this selectively reflects modern Western assumptions; supporters see responsible adaptation. Academic classification can describe these changes without deciding whether they constitute authentic Buddhism, a question communities answer differently.

nodes.title: Self-Realization Fellowship
nodes.summary: Paramahansa Yogananda's international organization teaching Kriya Yoga through a modern universalist Vedānta framework.
nodes.content:
# Self-Realization Fellowship

## Historical context

Yogananda founded the organization in the United States in 1920 after training in the Yogoda and Kriya Yoga lineage of Sri Yukteswar. Lectures, correspondence lessons, monastic communities, and *Autobiography of a Yogi* made it an influential channel for modern yoga and Vedānta worldwide.

## Distinctives and comparative notes

The movement teaches Kriya Yoga meditation, devotion, ethical discipline, and direct realization of God. Yogananda presented parallels between Krishna's and Jesus's teachings within a universalist theology. Its modern organizational form and transreligious language distinguish it from classical Yoga as a philosophical school.

nodes.title: Seon Buddhism
nodes.summary: Korean forms of Chan Buddhism emphasizing meditation, monastic discipline, and integration with doctrinal study.
nodes.content:
# Seon Buddhism

## Historical context

Meditation lineages reached Korea from Tang China and were remembered as the Nine Mountain Schools. During Goryeo, Jinul developed an influential synthesis of Seon practice and doctrinal learning at the retreat community of Suseonsa. Later suppression and revival, colonial rule, and postwar institutional divisions shaped modern Korean Seon.

## Distinctives and comparative notes

Seon often combines sudden awakening with gradual cultivation and uses *hwadu* inquiry focused on a critical phrase. Monastic meditation retreats coexist with liturgy, scripture, funerals, and lay devotion. Korean Buddhist temples also accommodated mountain-spirit and indigenous ritual imagery, but “syncretism” should describe particular practices rather than reduce Seon to shamanism.

nodes.title: Sephardic Judaism
nodes.summary: Rabbinic traditions associated with Iberian Jewry and the communities formed after the expulsions from Spain and Portugal.
nodes.content:
# Sephardic Judaism

## Historical development

Sephardic culture flourished among Jews of medieval Iberia through Hebrew poetry, philosophy, law, science, and engagement with Arabic and Romance societies. Expulsions and forced conversions in the late fifteenth century dispersed communities across North Africa, the Ottoman world, Italy, Western Europe, and the Americas.

## Practice and identity

Sephardic communities developed related liturgical rites, legal traditions, and languages including Ladino, while retaining marked regional diversity. “Sephardi” may denote Iberian ancestry, a prayer rite, or broader legal-cultural alignment. It overlaps with but should not simply replace the category Mizrahi, which encompasses many Middle Eastern communities without Iberian descent.

nodes.title: Serbian Orthodox Church
nodes.summary: An autocephalous Eastern Orthodox church associated historically with Serbian lands and the medieval patriarchate of Peć.
nodes.content:
# Serbian Orthodox Church

## Historical formation

Saint Sava obtained autocephaly for the Serbian church in 1219, linking ecclesiastical organization with the medieval Serbian state. The patriarchate of Peć underwent suppression and restoration under changing imperial regimes. In 1920 previously separated Serbian jurisdictions were reunited, and the patriarchal title was formally recognized again.

## Identity and governance

The church is organized synodally under the patriarch of Serbia and includes dioceses across the Balkans and diaspora. It follows Byzantine worship with a strong Church Slavonic and Serbian inheritance, while monasteries and the *slava* family-patron feast are culturally prominent. Its history intersects with national identity, but Eastern Orthodox ecclesiology cannot be reduced to ethnicity or state politics.

nodes.title: Serer Religion
nodes.summary: Inherited religious traditions of Serer communities in Senegal and The Gambia.
nodes.content:
# Serer Religion

## Historical context

Serer religious traditions developed within communities of present-day Senegal and The Gambia through kinship, land tenure, royal histories, farming, and inherited ritual offices. Islam, Christianity, colonial rule, migration, and national politics have produced varied contemporary identities. Oral transmission and localized sacred sites remain important; no written canon or central institution speaks for every Serer community.

## Distinctives and comparative notes

Roog, ancestral and saint-like *pangool*, maternal and paternal lineages, divination, initiation, and stewardship of land organize religious relationships in differing ways. The Saltigue diviners' public role is especially visible in some settings, but should not stand for the whole tradition. Serer practice deserves study on its own historical terms rather than as a generic “African animism” or a static precursor to neighboring religions.

nodes.title: Seventh Day Adventist Reform Movement
nodes.summary: An Adventist denomination formed during World War I over military service, Sabbath observance, and church discipline.
canonicalTexts: Seventh Day Adventist Reform Movement Principles of Faith
nodes.content:
# Seventh Day Adventist Reform Movement

## Historical development

The Reform Movement arose among European Seventh-day Adventists who rejected denominational accommodations to military service during World War I. After expulsions and failed reconciliation efforts, representatives organized internationally in the 1920s. A later division created separate organizations with similar historical claims, one retaining the Seventh Day Adventist Reform Movement name.

## Belief and practice

The movement preserves Seventh-day Adventist scripture, Sabbath, eschatology, and esteem for Ellen White while applying stricter teachings on noncombatancy, diet, dress, and church discipline. It regards itself as a reform within the Adventist inheritance, whereas the larger denomination treats it as a separate body. Its history should not be confused with unrelated Adventist reform initiatives.

nodes.title: Seventh-day Adventist Church
nodes.summary: The largest Adventist denomination, distinguished by Saturday Sabbath observance, global mission, and the influence of Ellen G. White.
nodes.content:
# Seventh-day Adventist Church

## Historical development

Seventh-day Adventism formed from Millerite believers who reinterpreted the disappointment of 1844 and adopted the seventh-day Sabbath. Networks associated with James and Ellen White, Joseph Bates, and other leaders organized the denomination in 1863. Publishing, education, medical institutions, and overseas mission made it the largest and most globally distributed Adventist body.

## Belief and practice

The church is Protestant and Trinitarian, observes Saturday as Sabbath, practices baptism by immersion, and teaches conditional immortality and a heavenly investigative judgment beginning in 1844. Ellen White's writings are regarded as a continuing prophetic gift while the Bible is identified as the doctrinal standard. Health practices and a strong educational system are prominent but vary among members and regions.

nodes.title: Shabak Religious Tradition
nodes.summary: The internally diverse religious traditions of Shabak communities in northern Iraq, shaped by Shi'i, Sufi, and neighboring esoteric currents.
canonicalTexts: Shabak sacred hymns and oral traditions
nodes.content:
# Shabak Religious Tradition

## Historical setting

Shabak communities have lived especially in the Nineveh plain of northern Iraq and speak an Iranian language variety alongside Arabic and Kurdish. Sources describe hereditary religious specialists, sacred *Buyruk* materials, communal rites, and reverence for figures important in Shi‘i and Sufi traditions. Persecution, displacement, and competing ethnic classifications have deeply affected modern community life.

## Identity and classification

Some Shabaks identify as Twelver Shi‘i Muslims, while others emphasize a distinct communal religion; external labels often fail to respect that diversity. Parallels with Yarsan and Alevi traditions have encouraged genealogical theories, but direct descent is not established. The branch link is therefore explicitly tentative and should be read as a comparative placement rather than a settled identity claim.

nodes.title: Shadhiliyya
nodes.summary: A major North African and Egyptian Sufi order tracing its lineage to Abu al-Hasan al-Shadhili.
nodes.content:
# Shadhiliyya

## Historical development

Abu al-Hasan al-Shadhili taught in the thirteenth-century Maghreb and Egypt, and disciples including Abu al-Abbas al-Mursi and Ibn Ata Allah systematized his path. Numerous branches spread through North and East Africa, the Middle East, the Indian Ocean, and contemporary Western Muslim communities.

## Teaching and practice

Shadhili traditions commonly emphasize remembrance, gratitude, reliance on God, and spiritual realization while remaining engaged in ordinary work and society. Litanies such as *Hizb al-Bahr* circulate beyond formal initiates. Darqawi, Alawi, Yashruti, and other branches differ substantially, so the name denotes a broad lineage family.

nodes.title: Shafi'i School
nodes.summary: A Sunni legal school associated with al-Shafi'i and widespread in East Africa, southern Arabia, and Southeast Asia.
nodes.content:
# Shafi'i School

## Historical context

Muhammad ibn Idris al-Shafi'i studied in Arabia and Iraq before teaching in Egypt in the early ninth century. Works attributed to his mature period helped systematize argument about Qur'an, prophetic sunna, consensus, and analogy. Scholarly and trading networks spread the school along Indian Ocean routes, producing strong communities from Yemen and East Africa to Indonesia.

## Distinctives and comparative notes

Shafi'i legal theory gives authenticated prophetic reports a central role and seeks disciplined analogical extension when explicit texts do not settle a case. Later jurists refined rather than merely repeated al-Shafi'i's positions. The school coexists with Ash'ari theology in many regions, but legal and theological affiliation remain different categories. Variation among the four Sunni schools represents accepted jurisprudential pluralism, not four separate religions.

nodes.title: Shamanic Traditions
nodes.summary: A comparative umbrella for specialized ritual mediation, healing, and spirit encounter, derived from a Siberian term but applied much more broadly.
nodes.content:
# Shamanic Traditions

## Historical context

The word *shaman* entered European scholarship through Tungusic-speaking communities of Siberia and was later extended to ritual specialists around the world. That expansion can enable comparison but has also erased local titles, institutions, and colonial histories. Contemporary “neo-shamanism” is a separate modern phenomenon and should not be silently substituted for Indigenous practice.

## Distinctives and comparative notes

Practices called shamanic may include spirit negotiation, healing, divination, soul journey, drumming, possession, or initiation through illness, but no universal checklist applies. Specialists operate within accountable communities and cosmologies. This node represents an analytical family resemblance, not a claim that all ritual mediators descend from one prehistoric religion.

nodes.title: Shangqing Daoism
nodes.summary: A medieval Daoist revelatory corpus and lineage emphasizing visualization, inner divinities, celestial journeys, and refined self-cultivation.
nodes.content:
# Shangqing Daoism

## Historical context

Between 364 and 370, Yang Xi recorded revelations said to come from perfected beings for members of the Xu family near modern Nanjing. Tao Hongjing later collected and ordered this material at Mount Mao, making Shangqing scripture prestigious at southern courts. Its texts and ritual imagery entered the broader Daoist canon and continued within later Maoshan transmission.

## Distinctives and comparative notes

Shangqing practice foregrounded the visualization of deities within the body, nocturnal celestial travel, recitation, dietary discipline, and individual meditation more than the communal rites characteristic of early Celestial Masters. Its revealed heavens and divine biographies created new maps of salvation. Scholars use “school” for a changing textual and initiatory current; it was never a denomination with a single continuous bureaucracy.

nodes.title: Shaykhism
nodes.summary: A Twelver Shia school founded through the teachings of Shaykh Ahmad al-Ahsa'i, emphasizing imamology and esoteric cosmology.
nodes.content:
# Shaykhism

## Historical development

Shaykh Ahmad al-Ahsa'i and his successor Sayyid Kazim Rashti formed a distinctive scholarly network in Qajar Iran and Ottoman Iraq. Their teachings explored the spiritual bodies of resurrection, the metaphysical rank of the imams, and layered worlds of divine manifestation. Leadership disputes after Rashti produced several continuing Shaykhi communities.

## Influence and distinction

Some students from the Shaykhi environment became early followers of the Bab, giving the school an important place in Babi history. Other Shaykhis rejected the Bab's claims and remained within Twelver Shiism. The influence edge therefore records a historical milieu rather than identifying Shaykhism itself as Babi or Bahá'í.

nodes.title: Shi'a Islam
nodes.summary: Islamic traditions centered on the authority of Ali and the Prophet's family, with several distinct lines of Imams.
nodes.content:
# Shi'a Islam

## Historical context

Shi'a traditions grew from loyalty to Ali ibn Abi Talib and claims that authority after Muhammad belonged within the Prophet's household. The killing of Husayn at Karbala in 680 became a defining memory of injustice and faithful witness. Disagreements over lines of Imams later produced Twelver, Ismaili, Zaydi, and other communities with distinct histories.

## Distinctives and comparative notes

Shi'a theology gives the Imams special authority as guides to revelation and law, although the nature and number of Imams differ by branch. Ritual remembrance of Karbala, devotion to the Prophet's family, pilgrimage, and separate hadith corpora are prominent. Shi'a and Sunni Muslims share the Qur'an, core worship, and many legal concepts. The schism edge visualizes a gradual political-theological differentiation, not a single instant of separation.

nodes.title: Shingon Buddhism
nodes.summary: A Japanese esoteric Buddhist tradition transmitted by Kūkai, using mantra, mudra, mandala, and ritual identification with awakening.
nodes.content:
# Shingon Buddhism

## Historical context

Kūkai returned from Tang China in 806 with esoteric initiations, texts, and ritual technologies that became Shingon. Mount Kōya and Tōji developed as major centers, while Shingon lineages served court, monastery, and local communities. The tradition adapted Indian and Chinese materials within Japanese institutional settings.

## Distinctives and comparative notes

Shingon presents Mahāvairocana Buddha as the cosmic expression of reality and uses the “three mysteries” of body, speech, and mind to realize buddhahood in this very body. Mandalas organize ritual worlds, but practice requires graded initiation. Kami were historically interpreted through Buddhist frameworks and worshiped in shared sites; this relationship changed under nineteenth-century separation policies.

nodes.title: Shinto
nodes.summary: Japanese traditions of shrine, community, imperial, and household relations with kami, ritual purity, place, and season.
nodes.content:
# Shinto

## Historical context

Practices concerning *kami* long preceded the label Shinto as a bounded religion. Court myth, local shrines, clan rites, pilgrimage, and agricultural festivals developed together with imported writing and institutions. For more than a millennium kami worship was frequently organized through Buddhist temples and theories until modern governments imposed administrative separation.

## Distinctives and comparative notes

Shrine rites cultivate proper relations with kami through purification, offerings, prayer, festival, and care for sacred places. Shinto has no single founder or universal creed; priestly organizations, local communities, imperial rites, and new movements differ. Describing kami simply as “gods” can mislead, since the category includes powerful presences associated with landscape, ancestors, events, and extraordinary persons.

nodes.title: Shipibo-Konibo Religious Traditions
nodes.summary: Shipibo-Konibo traditions of the Peruvian Amazon involving plant knowledge, healing songs, patterned design, kinship, riverine places, and spirit relations.
nodes.content:
# Shipibo-Konibo Religious Traditions

## Historical context

Shipibo, Konibo, and Xetebo communities formed a related people through long histories along the Ucayali and its tributaries. Missions, rubber extraction, epidemics, urban migration, oil and logging pressure, and global ayahuasca tourism changed healing economies and access to knowledge. Community artists, language teachers, healers, and organizations actively shape contemporary representation.

## Distinctives and comparative notes

Plants known as *rao*, healing songs, dreams, diets, river beings, and geometric *kené* designs participate in interconnected forms of knowledge and care. Ayahuasca is important in some practice but does not summarize Shipibo-Konibo religion or authorize outsiders to extract songs and designs. “Shamanism” is an external comparison; local specialist terms and lineage protocols are more precise.

nodes.title: Shona Religious Traditions
nodes.summary: Religious traditions among Shona-speaking communities involving Mwari, ancestors, territorial spirits, mediumship, rain, healing, and land.
nodes.content:
# Shona Religious Traditions

## Historical context

Shona-speaking societies in Zimbabwe and neighboring regions developed varied ritual systems around dynastic centers, local chiefdoms, agriculture, cattle, and sacred landscapes. The Mwari cult associated with Matobo held regional significance, while spirit mediums participated in resistance, community memory, and political negotiation. Christianity, colonial rule, liberation war, and urban migration have continually reshaped these roles.

## Distinctives and comparative notes

Ancestors, clan spirits, territorial *mhondoro*, and Mwari connect moral conduct with rain, fertility, health, and legitimate authority. Mediums may speak for historical or territorial beings, but their public power differs by place and period. “Shona religion” is a linguistic-regional umbrella rather than a centralized system, and political uses of spirit-medium history remain debated.

nodes.title: Shugendō
nodes.summary: A Japanese mountain-ascetic tradition integrating esoteric Buddhism, kami worship, pilgrimage, and demanding embodied practice.
nodes.content:
# Shugendō

## Historical context

Shugendō took shape around sacred mountains, itinerant practitioners called *yamabushi*, Buddhist temples, and local kami cults. Traditions associate the path with the legendary En no Gyōja. Esoteric Buddhist institutions systematized many rites, while regional pilgrimage circuits retained distinctive lineages. Meiji separation policies prohibited Shugendō temporarily, but communities later revived.

## Distinctives and comparative notes

Mountain entry, fasting, waterfall austerity, mantra, fire ritual, and guided pilgrimage transform the practitioner through direct encounter with a sacral landscape. Shugendō is paradigmatically combinatory, yet “syncretism” should not imply a random mixture: initiations, ranks, routes, and temple affiliations organize practice. Contemporary groups vary in accessibility and institutional connection.

nodes.title: Siberian Shamanic Traditions
nodes.summary: Community-specific ritual traditions across Siberia involving healing, spirit mediation, land relations, and specialist initiation.
nodes.content:
# Siberian Shamanic Traditions

## Historical context

Siberia contains many peoples and language families, including Evenki, Sakha, Buryat, Khanty, and others, whose ritual traditions cannot be collapsed into one system. Russian imperial rule, Orthodox missions, Soviet persecution, settlement, extractive industry, and post-Soviet revival transformed local institutions. The English word *shaman* ultimately derives from a Tungusic term.

## Distinctives and comparative notes

Depending on community, specialists may heal, retrieve souls, guide the dead, divine, mediate with land masters, or sustain clan relations through song, costume, drum, and offering. Similar techniques do not erase distinct cosmologies or political histories. This node groups a region for navigation while directing interpretation back toward specific peoples rather than an imagined pan-Siberian creed.

nodes.title: Sikh Dharma International / 3HO
nodes.summary: A transnational Sikh-derived community founded by Harbhajan Singh Khalsa, combining Khalsa identity with a branded Kundalini Yoga system.
nodes.content:
# Sikh Dharma International / 3HO

## Historical context

Harbhajan Singh, known as Yogi Bhajan, organized 3HO in North America from the late 1960s. Many converts adopted Sikh names, Khalsa discipline, gurdwara worship, and distinctive white clothing while teaching a modern system marketed as Kundalini Yoga. The movement built religious, educational, and commercial institutions.

## Distinctives and comparative notes

Members combine Sikh scripture and identity with yogic exercises and teachings not generally practiced in Punjabi Sikh communities. Its place within global Sikhism is contested, and investigations after the founder's death documented serious allegations of abuse. Describing the movement requires separating Sikh tradition, its modern yoga system, and institutional conduct.

nodes.title: Sikh Tradition
nodes.summary: A Punjab-origin religion founded through the Sikh Gurus, centered on the Guru Granth Sahib, divine remembrance, service, and justice.
nodes.content:
# Sikh Tradition

## Historical context

Guru Nanak taught in late fifteenth- and early sixteenth-century Punjab, and nine succeeding human Gurus developed a community, scripture, institutions, and public ethics. Guru Arjan compiled the Ādi Granth; Guru Gobind Singh founded the Khalsa and affirmed the scripture and community as enduring Guru. Sikh history later unfolded through empire, colonialism, reform, partition, and diaspora.

## Distinctives and comparative notes

Sikhs worship one ineffable God through remembrance of the divine Name, sung scripture, honest work, sharing, service, and resistance to oppression. The *gurdwara* and *langar* enact congregational equality. Sikh teaching arose amid Hindu bhakti and Islamic-Sufi worlds yet constitutes a self-defined tradition, not a hybrid or branch of either.

nodes.title: Siyam Nikāya
nodes.summary: A major Sri Lankan monastic fraternity established through an ordination mission from the Thai kingdom of Ayutthaya.
nodes.content:
# Siyam Nikāya

## Historical context

The Siyam Nikāya arose when the Kandyan court invited monks from Ayutthaya to restore higher ordination in 1753 under the leadership of the Thai monk Upāli. The mission renewed a lineage that Sri Lankan Buddhists considered interrupted and linked the Kandyan sangha to wider Theravāda networks. The fraternity subsequently divided into several chapters centered on important temples and teacher successions.

## Distinctives and comparative notes

The nikāya has preserved monastic education, ritual service, temple administration, and Pāli discipline within Sri Lankan Buddhism. Historically, access to its higher ordination was restricted largely to the Govigama caste, a policy that helped prompt the creation of other fraternities. The term “Siyam,” meaning Siamese, records the ordination connection; it does not make the fraternity an administrative branch of modern Thai Buddhism.

nodes.title: Slavic Religion
nodes.summary: The varied pre-Christian practices of Slavic-speaking communities in eastern, central, and southeastern Europe.
nodes.content:
# Slavic Religion

## Historical context

Pre-Christian Slavic religions are known through sparse archaeology, place-names, medieval chronicles, sermons against customary rites, and later folklore. Evidence differs markedly between Kievan Rus', the Baltic coast, western Slavic regions, and the Balkans. Most written witnesses are Christian and late, so a single original Slavic pantheon cannot be recovered with confidence from scattered divine names.

## Distinctives and comparative notes

Perun, Veles, household beings, ancestors, seasonal rites, oath-making, and agricultural observances are attested unevenly. Political rulers sometimes organized public cults, but village and domestic practice followed other rhythms. Folkloric survival is possible in particular cases, yet continuity must be shown rather than assumed. Contemporary Rodnovery builds modern ritual and identity from scholarship, folklore, nationalism, and creative reconstruction in varying proportions.

inbound.title: Rodnovery
inbound.citation: Kaarina Aitamurto, Paganism, Traditionalism, Nationalism (2016)

nodes.title: Smārta Tradition
nodes.summary: A Brahmanical Hindu tradition joining domestic orthopraxy, multiple-deity worship, and influential Advaita interpretation.
nodes.content:
# Smārta Tradition

## Historical context

“Smārta” has referred broadly to Brahmins oriented toward *smṛti* and domestic Vedic norms, and more narrowly to communities associated with Advaita Vedānta and Śaṅkara-linked monastic centers. The familiar five-shrine *pañcāyatana* pattern honors Śiva, Viṣṇu, Devī, Sūrya, and Gaṇeśa without requiring exclusive allegiance.

## Distinctives and comparative notes

Smārta practice combines household rites, temple worship, life-cycle observances, and philosophical study. Its inclusive deity arrangement is sometimes presented as a universal template for Hinduism, but it represents one historical formation among many. Advaita supplies an influential account of divine forms within nondual reality, yet not every Smārta practitioner is primarily philosophical, and multi-deity worship also occurs outside Smārta institutions.

nodes.title: So-Called Cargo Cult Movements
nodes.summary: A contested scholarly category for distinct Oceanic prophetic movements responding to colonial power and exchange.
nodes.content:
# So-Called Cargo Cult Movements

## Historical context

Anthropologists and colonial officials applied “cargo cult” to many unrelated prophetic, political, and ritual movements in Melanesia and nearby regions. These arose amid missionization, labor recruitment, racial hierarchy, war, and radically unequal access to wealth. Grouping them by an alleged desire for Western goods often made Indigenous theories of justice and sovereignty appear irrational while treating colonial extraction as normal.

## Distinctives and comparative notes

Particular movements used Christian prophecy, ancestors, kastom, new ritual, military imagery, or cooperative organization in different combinations. Some expected material transformation, but “cargo” was never their single concern. The node is minority-tier because scholars increasingly criticize the category itself. Users should navigate to named communities such as John Frum and interpret each movement through its own language, leaders, and political history.

inbound.title: John Frum Movement
inbound.citation: Lamont Lindstrom, Cargo Cult (1993)

outbound.title: Christianity
outbound.citation: Holger Jebens, ed., Cargo, Cult, and Culture Critique (2004)

nodes.title: Soka Gakkai
nodes.summary: A global lay Nichiren Buddhist movement emphasizing chanting, personal transformation, peace, culture, and education.
nodes.content:
# Soka Gakkai

## Historical context

Educators Makiguchi Tsunesaburō and Toda Jōsei founded the Soka Kyoiku Gakkai in 1930 within Nichiren Shōshū. Reorganized after wartime repression, Soka Gakkai grew rapidly under Toda and Ikeda Daisaku and developed an international network. Its institutional separation from Nichiren Shōshū in the 1990s made it an independent lay movement.

## Distinctives and comparative notes

Members chant *Nam-myōhō-renge-kyō* before a *gohonzon*, study Nichiren’s writings, and frame practice as “human revolution” expressed through daily life and social contribution. Peace, education, and cultural exchange are prominent public themes. Political involvement through Japan’s Komeito has generated debate; legal organizational ties and members’ political views require careful distinction.

nodes.title: Sōtō Zen
nodes.summary: Japan’s largest Zen school, rooted in Caodong transmission and shaped especially by Dōgen, Keizan, temple ritual, and seated practice.
nodes.content:
# Sōtō Zen

## Historical context

Dōgen returned from China in 1227 and established a Japanese lineage grounded in Caodong teaching; Eiheiji became an enduring center. Keizan Jōkin and later disciples expanded the network through rural temples, funerary service, devotion, and flexible transmission. Modern reforms systematized the school’s administration and promoted Dōgen’s writings in Japan and internationally.

## Distinctives and comparative notes

Sōtō discourse gives special weight to *shikantaza*, or “just sitting,” and to Dōgen’s claim that practice and realization are inseparable. Daily liturgy, precepts, work, memorial rites, and teacher-student transmission are equally integral to institutional life. The familiar contrast between contemplative Sōtō and kōan-centered Rinzai is incomplete: historical Sōtō teachers also used kōan literature, and most parish temples serve broad ritual roles.

nodes.title: Southern Baptist Convention
nodes.summary: A large United States Baptist convention founded in a sectional dispute over slaveholding missionaries and later shaped by evangelical conservatism.
nodes.content:
# Southern Baptist Convention

## Historical development

White Baptist churches organized the Southern Baptist Convention in 1845 after a national missionary body declined to appoint slaveholders as missionaries. Following the Civil War, the convention built mission boards, seminaries, and publishing institutions while African American Baptists formed independent conventions. Twentieth-century growth made it the largest Protestant denomination in the United States.

## Theology and structure

SBC congregations are autonomous but cooperate in conventions and support shared missions and education. The Baptist Faith and Message expresses conservative evangelical positions on scripture, baptism, Communion, and ministry, though it is not a binding creed over each church. The denomination has formally repudiated its defense of slavery while continuing to debate race, gender, abuse accountability, and political engagement.

nodes.title: Spiritism
nodes.summary: A movement codified by Allan Kardec that joins mediumship, reincarnation, moral progress, and a rationalized account of spirits.
nodes.content:
# Spiritism

## Historical context

French educator Hippolyte Léon Denizard Rivail, writing as Allan Kardec, organized reports of mediumistic communication into a systematic doctrine beginning in 1857. Spiritism spread especially strongly in Brazil, where associations, charities, healing practices, and publishing networks became major institutions.

## Distinctives and comparative notes

Spiritists teach survival after death, repeated incarnation, communication with spirits, moral causation, and progressive education across lives. Kardec distinguished his codified philosophy from the broader Spiritualist séance movement. Academic inclusion records a historical religion; it does not verify paranormal or medical claims.

nodes.title: Śramaṇa Movements
nodes.summary: An analytical umbrella for renunciant movements of ancient India that debated karma, rebirth, knowledge, austerity, and liberation outside Brahmanical household norms.
nodes.content:
# Śramaṇa Movements

## Historical context

During the first millennium BCE, renouncers, teachers, and communities in northern India developed alternatives to Vedic sacrifice and householder status. Buddhist and Jain sources preserve debates with Ājīvikas, materialists, skeptics, and other groups, although accounts written by rivals must be used critically.

## Distinctives and comparative notes

Śramaṇa is a broad social and historical category, not one religion. Its communities disagreed over whether karma exists, whether action changes destiny, what survives death, and whether knowledge or austerity liberates. Buddhism and Jainism became durable institutional traditions, while several contemporaries disappeared or survive mainly through hostile reports.

nodes.title: Sri Lankan Buddhism
nodes.summary: The Sri Lankan Theravāda tradition whose Pāli textual, monastic, and ritual lineages deeply shaped Buddhism across Southeast Asia.
nodes.content:
# Sri Lankan Buddhism

## Historical context

Buddhist chronicles connect the island’s first durable monastic establishment with missions during Aśoka’s reign in the third century BCE. Anurādhapura monasteries developed distinct fraternities, and the Mahāvihāra lineage eventually supplied the institutional ancestry claimed by modern Theravāda. Sri Lankan monks, manuscripts, relics, and ordination missions repeatedly circulated through mainland Southeast Asia, even as warfare and colonial rule disrupted local institutions.

## Distinctives and comparative notes

Sri Lankan practice joins Pāli learning and monastic discipline with pilgrimage, relic and bodhi-tree devotion, protective chanting, merit-making, and worship of regional deities. Modern reformers promoted lay meditation, print culture, education, and Buddhist nationalism in response to Christian missions and colonial government. “Sri Lankan Buddhism” is therefore a regional tradition containing multiple nikāyas and political outlooks, not a single centralized church.

nodes.title: Śrī Vaiṣṇavism
nodes.summary: A South Indian Vaiṣṇava tradition joining Tamil Āḻvār devotion, temple liturgy, and Viśiṣṭādvaita theology.
nodes.content:
# Śrī Vaiṣṇavism

## Historical context

Śrī Vaiṣṇavism developed in Tamil South India from temple traditions, the vernacular hymns of the Āḻvārs, and Sanskrit Vedānta. Nāthamuni, Yāmuna, and Rāmānuja helped consolidate its institutions and theology, while major centers such as Śrīraṅgam sustained ritual and scholastic lineages.

## Distinctives and comparative notes

Viṣṇu-Nārāyaṇa and Śrī are central, and salvation is understood through divine grace, surrender, devotion, and service. Sanskrit revelation and the Tamil *Divya Prabandham* function together as a “double Veda.” Later Vaṭakalai and Teṉkalai communities differ over grace, ritual, and interpretation without ceasing to belong to the wider tradition.

nodes.title: Śrīkula / Śrīvidyā
nodes.summary: A Śākta tantric family centered on Tripurasundarī, the Śrīcakra, mantra, and ordered worship of the beautiful Goddess.
nodes.content:
# Śrīkula / Śrīvidyā

## Historical context

Śrīvidyā systems matured in medieval South Asia and became important within South Indian temple, courtly, monastic, and household settings. They synthesize Goddess worship with carefully graded initiation and influential ritual diagrams, especially the Śrīcakra.

## Distinctives and comparative notes

Tripurasundarī is revered as supreme beauty and consciousness, expressed through mantra, the interlocking triangles of the Śrīcakra, and a retinue of divine powers. Ritual may be external, internalized through visualization, or interpreted philosophically. Distinct lineages transmit different mantra sequences and theological frameworks.

nodes.title: State Shinto
nodes.summary: The modern Japanese state system that administered shrines and imperial rites as public civic institutions rather than officially as religion.
nodes.content:
# State Shinto

## Historical context

After the Meiji Restoration, the government separated kami and buddhas, reorganized shrines, ranked priesthoods, and connected imperial rites with national education. Officials often designated shrine observance as nonreligious civic ceremony, enabling its public support while other religious bodies were regulated separately. The system was dismantled under the 1945 Shinto Directive.

## Distinctives and comparative notes

State Shinto was an administrative and ideological formation, not all Shinto practice between 1868 and 1945. Participation varied, and shrines retained local functions even as national symbolism intensified. Scholars debate the term’s precise scope, but agree that modern institutions transformed older rites. Distinguishing State Shinto from contemporary shrine practice avoids treating nationalism as Shinto’s timeless essence.

nodes.title: Sthānakavāsī Jainism
nodes.summary: A Śvetāmbara Jain reform tradition rejecting image worship and emphasizing scripture, ascetic discipline, and meeting-hall devotion.
nodes.content:
# Sthānakavāsī Jainism

## Historical context

Sthānakavāsī formation followed late medieval western Indian critiques associated with Loṅkā Śāh, who argued that the received Āgamas did not authorize image worship. Distinct mendicant lineages emerged over time, gathering in simple halls rather than temple sanctuaries. The movement became influential in Rajasthan, Gujarat, Punjab, and diasporic communities.

## Distinctives and comparative notes

Sthānakavāsīs emphasize meditation, preaching, ethical vows, canonical study, and careful nonviolence while rejecting temple images and related offerings. Mendicants may wear a mouth covering as a visible precaution against harming minute life. “Reform” does not mean reduced ritual: disciplined confession, fasting, calendrical observance, and teacher-lineage practice remain substantial.

nodes.title: Stoicism
nodes.summary: A Hellenistic philosophical tradition teaching life according to reason and nature within a providentially ordered cosmos.
nodes.content:
# Stoicism

## Historical setting

Zeno of Citium taught at the Painted Stoa in Athens around 300 BCE. Cleanthes, Chrysippus, and later Greek and Roman thinkers developed a systematic tradition of logic, physics, and ethics. Most early works survive only in fragments, while Seneca, Epictetus, and Marcus Aurelius offer influential but distinct imperial-era forms.

## Religious and philosophical scope

Stoics described a rational, living cosmos pervaded by divine *logos* or pneuma and emphasized virtue, disciplined judgment, providence, and human kinship. They interpreted traditional gods allegorically while participating in surrounding civic cultures. Stoicism is best classified as a philosophical school with religious cosmology and practices, not as a church or a synonym for emotional suppression.

nodes.title: Śuddhādvaita Vedānta
nodes.summary: Vallabha's 'pure nondualism,' which regards Kṛṣṇa, selves, and cosmos as real expressions of one divine reality.
nodes.content:
# Śuddhādvaita Vedānta

## Historical context

Vallabha articulated Śuddhādvaita in fifteenth- and sixteenth-century North India through commentaries on the *Brahma Sūtras* and *Bhāgavata Purāṇa*. His teaching supplied the theological foundation for Puṣṭimārga and continued through hereditary teachers and scholastic interpretation.

## Distinctives and comparative notes

Śuddhādvaita identifies Brahman with the personal, blissful Kṛṣṇa while affirming the reality of the universe as divine manifestation. Bondage results from obscured awareness rather than an unreal world, and grace-filled devotion restores participation in divine play. It differs from Śaṅkara's Advaita and from dualist Vedānta without fitting a simple midpoint between them.

nodes.title: Sufism
nodes.summary: Islamic traditions of spiritual discipline and divine remembrance transmitted through teachers, texts, and devotional paths.
nodes.content:
# Sufism

## Historical context

Sufism developed from early Muslim asceticism, prayer, ethical self-examination, and reflection on intimacy with God. By the medieval period, teaching lineages and orders such as the Qadiriyya, Chishtiyya, Shadhiliyya, and Naqshbandiyya organized instruction and social institutions across Africa and Eurasia. Poetry, pilgrimage, lodges, scholarship, and reform linked Sufis to many societies.

## Distinctives and comparative notes

Sufi paths cultivate remembrance (*dhikr*), sincerity, disciplined character, and awareness of God under a guide. Practices may include silent or vocal recitation, music, movement, retreat, and visitation of saints, but no single practice defines all Sufis. Sufism crosses Sunni and Shi'a boundaries rather than forming a third denomination. Some Salafi reformers criticize specific Sufi customs, while other Sunni scholars combine law, theology, and Sufi training.

nodes.title: Sumerian Religion
nodes.summary: The temple-centered religious traditions of Sumerian-speaking city-states in southern Mesopotamia.
nodes.content:
# Sumerian Religion

## Historical context

Sumerian-speaking communities of southern Mesopotamia developed temple institutions by the fourth millennium BCE. Cities such as Uruk, Ur, Nippur, Eridu, and Lagash honored overlapping but locally ordered pantheons. Evidence comes from temples, offerings, administrative tablets, hymns, laments, myths, and later scribal copies; it does not reveal a single creed shared unchanged across every city or period.

## Distinctives and comparative notes

Divine authority, civic prosperity, irrigation, kingship, and ritual labor were closely connected. Deities including An, Enlil, Enki, Inanna, Nanna, and Utu occupied changing constellations of power. Sumerian compositions profoundly shaped later Akkadian-language Mesopotamian literature, yet “Sumerian religion” is a scholarly umbrella. Similar flood or creation motifs elsewhere require contextual comparison and do not by themselves prove direct borrowing.

inbound.title: Akkadian Religion
inbound.citation: Benjamin R. Foster, Before the Muses, 3rd ed. (2005)

nodes.title: Sunni Islam
nodes.summary: The largest family within Islam, recognizing the early caliphal community and plural schools of law and theology.
nodes.content:
# Sunni Islam

## Historical context

Sunni identity emerged gradually from debates over leadership, civil war, communal authority, law, and hadith after Muhammad's death. The expression *ahl al-sunna wa-l-jama'a* came to mark commitment to prophetic precedent and the broad community. By the medieval period, several legal and theological schools provided durable institutions across a wide geographic range.

## Distinctives and comparative notes

Sunni Muslims generally recognize the first four caliphs as legitimate and ground practice in Qur'an, prophetic sunna, scholarly consensus, and disciplined legal reasoning. Hanafi, Maliki, Shafi'i, and Hanbali law coexist, as do Ash'ari, Maturidi, Athari, Sufi, Salafi, and other orientations. Sunni Islam has no single worldwide hierarchy. Its distinction from Shi'a Islam concerns authority and sacred history, not a wholly different scripture or God.

nodes.title: Śvetāmbara Jainism
nodes.summary: A major Jain tradition of white-robed mendicants preserving an Āgama canon and diverse temple and reform lineages.
nodes.content:
# Śvetāmbara Jainism

## Historical context

Śvetāmbara institutions developed principally in western and northern India through mendicant orders, lay patronage, pilgrimage centers, manuscript culture, and scholastic debate. A council remembered at Valabhī is traditionally associated with reducing the transmitted Āgamas to writing, although historians treat details of the canon’s formation cautiously.

## Distinctives and comparative notes

Śvetāmbara monks and nuns wear white robes and the tradition accepts that women can attain liberation. Image-worshiping temple communities coexist with Sthānakavāsī and Terāpanth non-image lineages. Differences from Digambara Jainism include scripture, mendicant discipline, and narratives about liberated beings, while core commitments to Jinas, nonviolence, karma, and vows remain shared.

nodes.title: Swaminarayan Sampradāya
nodes.summary: A Gujarati Vaiṣṇava tradition founded around Sahajānand Swami, revered as Swaminarayan, with several modern institutional branches.
nodes.content:
# Swaminarayan Sampradāya

## Historical context

Sahajānand Swami organized the movement in early nineteenth-century Gujarat and came to be worshipped by followers as Swaminarayan. Temples, monastic leadership, moral codes, vernacular teaching, and social service supported durable communities. Succession produced multiple bodies, including the original diocesan organization and BAPS.

## Distinctives and comparative notes

The tradition combines disciplined Vaiṣṇava devotion, image worship, ethical vows, and reverence for an authorized lineage of teachers. Its branches differ over succession and the theological status of the guru. “Swaminarayan” therefore names a religious family rather than only one contemporary institution.

nodes.title: Syriac Catholic Church
nodes.summary: A West Syriac Catholic patriarchal church centered historically in the Middle East and in communion with Rome.
nodes.content:
# Syriac Catholic Church

## Historical formation

Pro-Catholic currents appeared within the Syriac Orthodox milieu during the early modern period, aided by contacts with missionaries and Rome. A lasting Catholic patriarchal succession is conventionally dated from the election of Michael Jarweh in 1782. Communities developed in present-day Syria, Lebanon, and Iraq before persecution, war, and migration produced a wide diaspora.

## Identity and practice

This patriarchal *sui iuris* church celebrates the West Syriac rite and preserves Syriac language, hymnody, fasting, and spirituality associated with Antiochene Christianity. It shares this broad ritual family with the Syriac Orthodox Church but belongs to the Catholic communion. It should not be confused with the Chaldean Catholic Church, which follows the distinct East Syriac tradition.

nodes.title: Syriac Orthodoxy
nodes.summary: A West Syriac Oriental Orthodox church historically centered around Antioch and Upper Mesopotamia.
nodes.content:
# Syriac Orthodoxy

## Historical context

The Syriac Orthodox Church carries a West Syriac Christian inheritance associated with Antioch. After the Council of Chalcedon, non-Chalcedonian communities endured imperial pressure and were reorganized through leaders including Jacob Baradaeus. Syriac scholarship, monasteries, and translation flourished across the Middle East and India. Violence in the late Ottoman period and modern displacement created a substantial diaspora.

## Distinctives and comparative notes

Worship uses the West Syriac rite and preserves Syriac, a literary form of Aramaic, alongside local languages. The church's miaphysite Christology aligns it with Oriental Orthodoxy. It differs from the East Syriac Church of the East in liturgy and historical ecclesiology, despite their shared linguistic world. The Malankara Syriac Orthodox tradition in India remains linked to the patriarch of Antioch.

nodes.title: Syro-Malabar Church
nodes.summary: An East Syriac major archiepiscopal Catholic church rooted among the Saint Thomas Christians of Kerala, India.
canonicalTexts: Holy Qurbana of Addai and Mari
nodes.content:
# Syro-Malabar Church

## Historical formation

The Syro-Malabar Church descends from the Saint Thomas Christian communities of India, which maintained long relationships with East Syriac bishops and merchants. Portuguese colonial intervention and the Synod of Diamper in 1599 brought stronger Latin oversight and liturgical alteration. Later restoration movements and independent hierarchy produced the modern major archiepiscopal church.

## Identity and practice

Syro-Malabar worship belongs to the East Syriac tradition and centers on the Holy Qurbana. The church is Indian and Catholic, not a migrant branch founded by European missionaries, though colonial encounters deeply affected it. It should also be distinguished from the Syro-Malankara Church, which follows the West Syriac rite, and from non-Catholic Saint Thomas Christian churches with related histories.

nodes.title: Syro-Malankara Catholic Church
nodes.summary: A West Syriac Eastern Catholic church formed through reunion by part of the Malankara Christian community in India.
nodes.content:
# Syro-Malankara Catholic Church

## Historical formation

The church arose when Archbishop Mar Ivanios and companions from the Malankara tradition entered communion with Rome in 1930. Their communities belonged to the complex history of the Saint Thomas Christians and had received the West Syriac liturgical tradition through connections with the Syriac Orthodox Church. A distinct hierarchy expanded in Kerala and through later diaspora.

## Identity and practice

The Syro-Malankara Catholic Church is a major archiepiscopal *sui iuris* church celebrating the West Syriac rite, especially the Liturgy of Saint James. Its name does not make it interchangeable with the Syro-Malabar Church, whose rite is East Syriac. Nor is it the same institution as the Malankara Orthodox Syrian Church, although both share elements of language, region, and West Syriac heritage.

nodes.title: Tannaitic Judaism
nodes.summary: The formative rabbinic culture of the tannaim, whose legal traditions were compiled in the Mishnah and related works.
nodes.content:
# Tannaitic Judaism

## Historical setting

The tannaim were rabbinic teachers active mainly in Roman Palestine from the late first through early third centuries CE. In the aftermath of the temple's destruction and the Bar Kokhba revolt, their circles transmitted and debated oral legal traditions concerning ritual, civil life, agriculture, festivals, and purity.

## Textual legacy

The Mishnah, traditionally associated with Judah ha-Nasi around 200 CE, became the foundational collection of tannaitic teaching. The Tosefta and tannaitic midrash preserve parallel and supplementary traditions. Scholars debate how widely early rabbis represented Jewish society, but their literary program became central to later rabbinic Judaism.

nodes.title: Tāraṇapantha
nodes.summary: A non-image-worshipping Digambara Jain tradition inspired by Tāraṇ Svāmī and centered on scripture halls and contemplative teaching.
nodes.content:
# Tāraṇapantha

## Historical context

Tāraṇ Svāmī taught in central India around the late fifteenth and early sixteenth centuries. Communities gathered around his writings and built *chaityālayas* that enshrine books rather than Jina images. The tradition remains regionally concentrated but historically important in Digambara reform.

## Distinctives and comparative notes

Tāraṇapanth worship emphasizes knowledge, meditation, ethical discipline, and reverence for texts. Its rejection of image ritual differentiates it from many Digambara temple traditions while leaving it within Jain commitments to the Jinas, karma theory, nonviolence, and liberation.

nodes.title: Tayyibi Ismailism
nodes.summary: The surviving Musta'li Ismaili tradition recognizing al-Tayyib as concealed imam and a succession of unrestricted missionaries.
nodes.content:
# Tayyibi Ismailism

## Historical development

Tayyibis recognized the infant al-Tayyib as imam after the death of the Fatimid caliph al-Amir and held that he entered concealment. Queen Arwa al-Sulayhi supported a Yemeni missionary hierarchy led by the *da'i al-mutlaq*, who guides the community on behalf of the hidden imam. The tradition later established a durable center in western India.

## Community structure

Tayyibi thought preserves Fatimid-Ismaili esoteric interpretation, ritual life, and a ranked missionary organization. Disputes over succession to the office of *da'i* produced Dawoodi, Sulaymani, Alavi, and other Bohra communities. They share a religious genealogy while maintaining separate leaders and institutions.

nodes.title: Temple of Set
nodes.summary: An initiatory Left-Hand Path religion founded by Michael Aquino that understands Set as a real principle of isolate intelligence.
canonicalTexts: The Book of Coming Forth by Night
nodes.content:
# Temple of Set

## Historical context

Michael Aquino and associates formed the Temple of Set in 1975 after leaving the Church of Satan. The organization developed a graded initiatory system drawing on ceremonial magic, Western esotericism, and a reinterpretation of the Egyptian deity Set. Its internal schools, called Orders, pursue specialized forms of study and practice.

## Distinctives and comparative notes

Setians generally affirm Set as an objective metaphysical intelligence and pursue *xeper*, self-directed becoming or coming into being. This distinguishes the Temple's theology from the Church of Satan's symbolic atheism. Its use of Egyptian names is a modern esoteric reception, not continuity with ancient Egyptian priesthood, and should be differentiated from reconstructionist Kemetism.

nodes.title: Tendai Buddhism
nodes.summary: The Japanese transmission of Tiantai centered at Mount Hiei, historically integrating Lotus, meditation, esoteric, and devotional practices.
nodes.content:
# Tendai Buddhism

## Historical context

Saichō established Japanese Tendai at Mount Hiei after studying Tiantai materials in China in the early ninth century. The institution developed its own ordination platform and combined Lotus teaching, meditation, Pure Land devotion, and esoteric ritual. Many founders of later Japanese schools first trained within its broad curriculum.

## Distinctives and comparative notes

Tendai affirms the potential for awakening in all beings and reads diverse practices through the unifying horizon of the *Lotus Sūtra*. Its doctrine of original enlightenment became influential but took several forms. Exchange and rivalry with Shingon shaped Japanese esoteric practice, while long entanglement with kami cults preceded modern efforts to administratively separate Buddhism and Shinto.

nodes.title: Tengrism
nodes.summary: Inner Asian religious traditions centered on Heaven or Tengri, land-and-water powers, ancestors, sovereignty, and ritual specialists.
canonicalTexts: The Secret History of the Mongols
nodes.content:
# Tengrism

## Historical context

Turkic and Mongolic polities of Inner Asia invoked Tengri, often translated as Eternal Heaven, in inscriptions and accounts of legitimate rule. Practices also concerned earth-water powers, ancestors, sacred mountains, fire, and divination. Islam, Buddhism, Christianity, imperial politics, and local traditions interacted with these complexes over many centuries.

## Distinctives and comparative notes

Tengrism is a modern umbrella whose historical referents were diverse and rarely constituted a centralized creed. Contemporary revival movements reconstruct identity from inscriptions, folklore, and living customs and should be distinguished from early imperial religion. “Sky god” comparisons can be useful, but they do not prove that Tengri is simply another culture's deity under a different name.

nodes.title: Tenrikyo
nodes.summary: A Japanese religion founded through Nakayama Miki's revelations, teaching joyful life, divine parenthood, service, and ritual healing.
nodes.content:
# Tenrikyo

## Historical context

Tenrikyo dates its founding to Nakayama Miki’s revelatory experience in 1838 at what became Jiba, the tradition’s sacred center in Nara. The community grew through healing, pilgrimage, song, and missionary networks. Meiji regulation compelled institutional association with Sect Shinto, from which Tenrikyo gained legal independence after World War II.

## Distinctives and comparative notes

God the Parent created humanity for the Joyous Life, realized through gratitude, mutual help, inner transformation, and *hinokishin* service. The seated service and sacred dances embody its revealed teaching. Its branch link records historical classification, not a claim that current adherents understand Tenrikyo merely as Shinto; the tradition maintains its own founder, scriptures, cosmology, and global institutions.

nodes.title: Terāpanth Jainism
nodes.summary: A centralized Sthānakavāsī-derived Jain order founded by Ācārya Bhikṣu, known for disciplined leadership and modern lay programs.
nodes.content:
# Terāpanth Jainism

## Historical context

Ācārya Bhikṣu founded the Śvetāmbara Terāpanth in Rajasthan in 1760 after disagreements over mendicant authority and conduct. The order developed an unusually centralized structure under one ācārya. In the twentieth century Ācārya Tulsi and Ācārya Mahāprajña expanded education, lay ethics, meditation, and international outreach.

## Distinctives and comparative notes

Terāpanth rejects image worship in continuity with Sthānakavāsī practice and stresses unified discipline, study, and obedience within the mendicant order. The Anuvrat movement invites people beyond Jainism to undertake small ethical vows, while Preksha meditation presents contemplative training in accessible form. These modern programs adapt Jain nonviolence without replacing the community’s canonical and ascetic foundations.

nodes.title: Thai Buddhism
nodes.summary: Thailand’s Theravāda traditions, encompassing the Mahā Nikāya and Dhammayut orders, temple communities, forest lineages, and popular devotion.
canonicalTexts: Thai monastic law and teaching collections
nodes.content:
# Thai Buddhism

## Historical context

Theravāda lineages connected with Sri Lanka became prominent in the Tai kingdoms of Sukhothai, Lanna, and Ayutthaya, although earlier Buddhist traditions also shaped the region. Kings patronized monasteries and presented themselves as defenders of the religion. Nineteenth- and twentieth-century governments centralized monastic administration, while forest teachers and urban reformers created influential alternatives within the same national field.

## Distinctives and comparative notes

Ordination, almsgiving, festivals, protective ritual, meditation, relic devotion, and temporary male monasticism all contribute to Thai Buddhist life. Most monks belong to either the majority Mahā Nikāya or the smaller Dhammayut order, though local practice exceeds these administrative categories. Relations with spirit cults and Brahmanical court ritual are layered and situational, so “syncretism” should not imply that participants experience a confused or incoherent religion.

nodes.title: Thai Forest Tradition
nodes.summary: A Thai Theravāda reform lineage emphasizing ascetic discipline, meditation, wandering practice, and direct training under teachers.
nodes.content:
# Thai Forest Tradition

## Historical context

The Kammaṭṭhāna or Thai Forest tradition formed around Ajahn Sao and Ajahn Mun in late nineteenth- and early twentieth-century northeastern Thailand. Its teachers renewed wandering ascetic observances and intensive meditation during a period when state-backed monastic administration was consolidating. Disciples later founded forest monasteries across Thailand and internationally.

## Distinctives and comparative notes

Practice emphasizes the Vinaya, selected ascetic observances, mindfulness of the body, concentration, and investigation of impermanence. Charismatic teacher narratives and relic devotion coexist with claims of experiential verification. “Forest” names an ideal and lineage, not a guarantee that every monastery is remote. The tradition is one modern Theravāda formation rather than an unchanged survival from the Buddha’s lifetime.

nodes.title: The Church of Jesus Christ (Bickertonite)
nodes.summary: A Latter Day Saint church descending from Sidney Rigdon and William Bickerton, with headquarters in Pennsylvania.
nodes.content:
# The Church of Jesus Christ (Bickertonite)

## Historical development

This church traces its succession through Sidney Rigdon's post-1844 claim and the ministry of William Bickerton in western Pennsylvania. Bickerton organized the body in 1862 after Rigdon's organization had fragmented. The parenthetical scholarly label “Bickertonite” distinguishes it from other churches with the same official name but is not normally part of the church's self-designation.

## Belief and practice

The church accepts the Bible and Book of Mormon while rejecting the Doctrine and Covenants and Pearl of Great Price as standards of scripture. It practices baptism by immersion, foot washing, Communion with bread and wine, and leadership by apostles and elders. It rejects plural marriage and several distinctive doctrines associated with the Utah-based Latter-day Saint tradition.

nodes.title: The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints
nodes.summary: The largest Latter Day Saint church, led west after Joseph Smith's death and headquartered in Salt Lake City.
canonicalTexts: King James Version of the Bible
nodes.content:
# The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints

## Historical development

After Joseph Smith's death in 1844, most Latter Day Saints who accepted the leadership of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles followed Brigham Young to the Great Basin. The Utah-based church developed a worldwide missionary system, temples, lay congregational leadership, and extensive educational and welfare institutions. It discontinued authorization of new plural marriages around the turn of the twentieth century and today is by far the movement's largest body.

## Belief and practice

Members affirm continuing revelation, restored priesthood authority, baptism and confirmation, temple covenants, eternal families, and the potential for human exaltation through Jesus Christ. Alongside the Bible, the church recognizes the Book of Mormon, Doctrine and Covenants, and Pearl of Great Price as scripture. “Mormon” remains historically familiar, but the church asks that its full name or “the Church of Jesus Christ” be used in most current references.

nodes.title: The Episcopal Church
nodes.summary: The United States-based province of the Anglican Communion, organized after American independence.
canonicalTexts: Constitution and Canons of The Episcopal Church
nodes.content:
# The Episcopal Church

## Historical development

Anglican congregations in the newly independent United States reorganized without royal supremacy and secured an episcopate through Scottish and English consecrations. A constitution and American Book of Common Prayer were adopted in 1789. The church later expanded through domestic and overseas missions and became an autonomous province of the Anglican Communion.

## Theology and governance

The Episcopal Church retains bishops, priests, deacons, liturgical worship, creeds, and Anglican comprehensiveness. General Convention joins a House of Bishops with elected clerical and lay deputies. It ordains women and LGBTQ clergy and authorizes same-sex marriage, decisions that have contributed to disputes and institutional separations within wider Anglicanism.

nodes.title: The Fourth Way
nodes.summary: G. I. Gurdjieff's modern esoteric teaching of awakening through self-observation, intentional work, movement, and group discipline in ordinary life.
nodes.content:
# The Fourth Way

## Historical context

G. I. Gurdjieff taught in Russia and Western Europe in the early twentieth century, later establishing an institute near Paris. P. D. Ouspensky's writings spread a related presentation, and multiple foundations and independent lineages continued after both teachers died.

## Distinctives and comparative notes

The teaching describes ordinary human beings as mechanically asleep and prescribes self-remembering, observation, sacred dance, music, and coordinated work. The “fourth way” is said to integrate bodily, emotional, and intellectual disciplines without monastic withdrawal. Claims of ancient hidden origins are difficult to verify and should be distinguished from the well-documented modern movement.

nodes.title: The New Church (Swedenborgianism)
nodes.summary: Christian churches inspired by Emanuel Swedenborg's visionary biblical theology, collectively known as the New Church.
nodes.content:
# The New Church (Swedenborgianism)

## Historical development

Emanuel Swedenborg published extensive accounts of visions and a spiritual interpretation of Christianity in the eighteenth century but did not found a denomination. Readers organized the first New Church body in London in 1787, followed by congregations in Europe and North America. Later divisions produced several Swedenborgian denominations with differing liturgies and institutional styles.

## Belief and practice

New Church theology understands the Trinity as united in the one person of Jesus Christ and interprets scripture through correspondences between natural and spiritual realities. It teaches continuing spiritual development, a freely chosen heaven or hell, and a new Christian age signified by the New Jerusalem. Worship and sacramental practice vary across Swedenborgian organizations, all of which regard Swedenborg's works as interpretive rather than an additional biblical canon.

nodes.title: The Satanic Temple
nodes.summary: A nontheistic Satanic organization using Satan as a symbol of rebellion, bodily autonomy, pluralism, and reason.
nodes.content:
# The Satanic Temple

## Historical context

The Satanic Temple appeared in the United States in 2013 and became known through public campaigns concerning religious pluralism, church-state separation, and bodily autonomy. It developed congregations, rituals, legal advocacy, and a formal set of ethical tenets.

## Distinctives and comparative notes

TST is nontheistic: Satan functions as a literary emblem rather than a supernatural being. Its activism is also lived by members as religious identity and community. It differs institutionally and philosophically from the Church of Satan, and neither represents historical accusations of devil worship made against minority groups.

nodes.title: Thelema
nodes.summary: An esoteric religious current founded by Aleister Crowley around the law of Thelema, ritual attainment, and discovery of True Will.
nodes.content:
# Thelema

## Historical context

Aleister Crowley founded Thelema after the 1904 reception of *The Book of the Law*, which he attributed to a discarnate intelligence named Aiwass. Crowley reworked ceremonial magic, yoga, mysticism, and initiatory orders into a new religious system. Thelemic communities now include several organizations and unaffiliated practitioners.

## Distinctives and comparative notes

The maxim “Do what thou wilt” refers within Thelema to discovering and enacting True Will, not simply following impulse. Ritual magic, meditation, graded initiation, sacred sexuality, and devotion to figures such as Nuit, Hadit, and Ra-Hoor-Khuit may feature. Claims about revelation are theological; the movement's historical debt to the Hermetic Order of the Golden Dawn and broader esotericism is documented.

nodes.title: Theodism
nodes.summary: A small modern Heathen current reconstructing Germanic sacral kingship, oath-bound community, and hierarchical customary relationships.
nodes.content:
# Theodism

## Modern formation

Theodism emerged in the United States during the 1970s as a distinctive current of Germanic neopaganism. Groups attempted to reconstruct an oath-bound *théod*, or people, using interpretations of Anglo-Saxon lordship, gift exchange, household cult, and sacral authority. Its history includes multiple organizations, schisms, and changes in self-description.

## Scope and distinction

Theodism is much smaller and more hierarchically structured than most Heathen organizations. Its reconstructed social order is a modern religious project, not the transparent continuation of a documented ancient institution. Not all Anglo-Saxon Heathens are Theodish, and many Heathens reject its hierarchy while sharing some source materials or divine names.

nodes.title: Theosophy
nodes.summary: A transnational esoteric movement seeking universal wisdom through occult evolution and selective readings of Asian and Western traditions.
nodes.content:
# Theosophy

## Historical context

Helena Blavatsky, Henry Steel Olcott, and associates founded the Theosophical Society in New York in 1875. Its center later moved to India, where members engaged Buddhist and Hindu reformers as well as anticolonial and educational projects. Successor organizations and disputes developed around leadership, revelation, and expected world teachers.

## Distinctives and comparative notes

Theosophy teaches spiritual evolution, karma, rebirth, hidden adepts, layered human constitution, and an ancient wisdom underlying religions. Its creative use of Sanskrit and Buddhist vocabulary helped popularize Asian traditions in Euro-American settings while often transforming them through occult and racial-evolutionary frameworks. Historical influence is clear; theological claims about primordial wisdom or masters remain confessional rather than academically established.

nodes.title: Theravāda Buddhism
nodes.summary: A living Buddhist tradition grounded in the Pāli canon and monastic lineages of Sri Lanka and mainland Southeast Asia.
nodes.content:
# Theravāda Buddhism

## Historical context
